heads of the Non-Plan expenditure and make concerted efforts for further saving in view of
the technological advancements in Government work establishments that cut on the requirements
of man power and resources, compared to yester-years. The Committee hopes that with
modernization of offices, the Non-Plan expenditure of these Departments can be curtailed
further so as to enhance the Plan projections and undertake more progressive and developmental
schemes and projects. The Committee, however, does not advocate reduction in plan funds at
the cost of efficient office management and service delivery. [Para 2.10.]
2. As regards the Plan projections, the Committee appreciates that the Ministry of
Finance has allocated funds to the Ministry as sought by it. The schemes and projects proposed
to be undertaken by the Departments in 2013-14 are also commendable. The Committee
therefore, desires that the three Departments of the Ministry of Law and Justice should make
concerted efforts to realize the goals set by them for the financial year and closely monitor
the implementation of the schemes and projects funded by them. The Committee, however,
cautions the Departments that they should take a pro active stance in the execution and
realization of the goals under the schemes and projects of the spending units under their
administrative jurisdiction and not merely play the role of the fund disbursing agency. The
Committee is hopeful that the Plan side of the demands for grants of the Ministry will go a
long way in bringing about better delivery of services. [Para 2.11]
3. The Committee appreciates the SVEEP programme under-taken by the Commission and
hopes that the programme will fill up the existing gaps in the education and empowerment of
the voters by creating awareness, especially among the rural, deprived and women in particular
so as to make the democracy more vibrant. However, the Committee feels that the actual
target of voters awareness programme should be clearly defined so that the countries valuable
resources do not go waste. It should accordingly, implement the programme in a pre-determined
phased manner beginning with States nearer to elections. [Para 3.8]
4. Another important area of concern is the use of EVMs in the elections. An elector has
every right to know whether the candidate to whom he has cast his vote through the electronic
voting machine has actually gone for that candidate. This is not possible in the present system.
The Election Commission has reported that they are in the process of attaching printer to the
EVM on a limited scale for giving a printed copy of the vote cast by the elector at the polling
station. The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Election Commission of India
to give a printed confirmation of the vote he has cast for the candidate of his/her choice to
confirm that no manipulation in the voting machine has occurred after the vote has been cast
by the elector. The Committee hopes that this measure of the Election Commission would go
a long way in establishing the faith of the electors in the EVMs and the processes in the
conduct of the elections. [Para 3.9]
54

55
5. The Committee takes note of the decrease in the budgetary proposals under heads such
as ‘Other Administrative Expenses’ and Major Works ‘Domestic Travel Expenses’ by R25 lakh
and R4 crore, respectively, from RE 2012-13 to BE 2013-14 in compliance with the guidelines
of the Ministry of Finance regarding observance of austerity measures in expenditure. The
Committee appreciates the efficient use of Grants under these heads by the Commission and
hopes that this would not have any adverse impact on the functional efficiency of the
Commission. [Para 3.10]
6. The Committee appreciates the establishment of IIIDEM and its objective i.e. training
of both India and foreign electoral officials. However, the Committee fails to comprehend the
decrease in financial allocation from R5 crore in RE (2012-13) to R1 crore in BE (2013-14)
when the need to make the campus of the Institute efficient, adequate and competently
operational is so urgent. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Institute should not
come across any constraint of funds at any stage and if they feel necessary, they may review
their requirement at the RE stage. [Para 3.13]
7. The Committee appreciates the steps undertaken to increase the NRI voter’s registration.
However, it feels that more concrete steps are needed for this, the Commission may plan,
accordingly. The Committee also notes the facilities provided to the Election observers and it
feels that the facilities like accommodation, transport TA, DA, etc should rather be made by
the Election Commission itself so that the observers could function in an impartial manner.
[Para 3.17]
8. The Committee notes the submissions of the Election Commission. It, however, reiterate
its earlier recommendation on the issue and accordingly, urges the Government and ECI to
review the Model Code of Conduct. In this context, the Committee recommends deletion of
para 16A of the Election Symbols (Reservation & Allotment) Order, 1968, and incorporate the
same in the Representation of People Act, 1951. The Committee also takes up this opportunity
to observe that the Code of Conduct be made effective from the date of Press Note/Press
Conference declaring the elections. The Committee, in this context, recommends that the Code
of Conduct should be made effective from the date of notification of elections and not from
the date of the declarations of the elections. [Para 3.21]
9. The Committee appreciates the steps undertaken by the Commission for EPIC coverage
in States like Assam, J&K and Nagaland in order to have 100 percent EPIC there. The
Committee hopes that the Election Commission would achieve the target of 100 percent before
the next general election. Amidst all the drawbacks and constraints that exist, the Committee
notes with appreciation the impressive EPIC coverage in the country. [Para 3.26]
10. The Committee desires that the photo quality of the present Elector Voter Identity
Card be improved for the benefit and the convenience of the voters and the implementing
agencies. [Para 3.28]
11. The Committee notes the view point of the Election Commission that the issue of
e-voting need to be studied and researched in larger depth and it may not be introduced as
of now. As regards the use of EVMs, the Committee desires that records of cases of mal-
function and tempering of EVMs as pointed out by Members, if so occurred, may be kept so
that concrete steps can be taken to rectify the specific shortcoming. The Committee, incidentally
also recommends that the mock voting done through EVMs should be made transparent.
[Para 3.34]

56
12. ........The Committee recommends to the Election Commission to initiate steps to
create awareness and education among the electors so that their participation in the election
process is voluntary, to the maximum, constructive and in the right prospective. This
will further deepen the roots of democratic set up in our country which is our asset.
[Para 3.35]
13. Keeping in mind the current level of literacy level and awareness of the voters, the
Committee desires that the nomination filing process work be made simple so as to avoid
unnecessary paper work and harassment to the candidates. [Para 3.36]
14. Committee is seriously concerned about the pending vacancy of Chairperson, and feels
that it may severely affect the working of important body like the Appellate Tribunal for
Foreign Exchange (ATFE). The Committee urges the Ministry to immediately fill up the
existing vacancies in ATFE so that the work may not be compromised. [Para 4.5]
15. The Committee expresses its concern over the mounting pendency in the Income Tax
Appellate Tribunal (ITAT). The inability for some Benches to function regularly due to
vacancies in the posts of Members is seen as totally undesirable by the Committee. Accordingly,
the Committee urges the Department and the ITAT to make timely and concerted efforts in
filling up the vacancies. The Committee feels that the filling–up of the vacancies, both in the
higher and lower grades along with the computerization of ITAT will go a long way in reducing
the pendency of cases. Thus, the Committee recommends that the vacant posts in ITAT be
filled up within a period of three months. [Para 4.12]
16. At the same time, the Committee appreciates the introduction of e-courts and
e-Benches connecting Nagpur Bench and Mumbai Bench. It desires that other Benches should
also be connected so that appeals of similar nature pending in various Benches could be heard
in one sitting. [Para 4.13]
17. The progressive increase in budget for National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) is a
welcome initiative although the allocation has been slightly lower than the actual demand made
by the NALSA. The Committee understands the role of legal awareness in a democratic
country like India and hopes that NALSA will keep-up its role of promoting legal awareness
and providing legal aid during the current financial year also. It recommends that a roadmap
and time frame may be drawn up for the implementation of its programs. The Committee
hopes that assessment of the impact of the working of Legal Aid Clinics and Para Legal
Volunteers, which is being done by NALSA periodically, will give an insight into areas that call
for improvement to the Government. [Para 4.19]
18. The Committee appreciates the activities of the BCI and takes cognizance of the
schemes and programmes proposed to be taken up by it in 2013-14. The BCI had proposed
R5 crore for the establishment of ‘Central Law library’. The Committee however, is of the
view that instead of a new library, the BCI should establish an online database of law libraries
and establish a sharing mechanism with the existing libraries for optimum utilization of the
resources. The Committee appreciates the proposal of setting up the ‘Directorate of Legal
Education’ and desires that operational details of the proposal be worked out for its efficient
implementation by the Ministry. [Para 4.25]
19. The Committee also takes note of the new One Year LLM programme introduced by
University Grants Commission and desires that BCI should help introduce this programme in
different law institutes/universities. [Para 4.26]

57
20. The Committee also takes note of the journal ‘Indian Bar Review’ brought out by the
BCI. However, the Committee expresses its disappointment that the Journal has only 480
subscribers, despite being more than 30 years old. The BCI may make efforts to popularize
and increase its subscription base and also undertake some research works for the promotion
of legal education. [Para 4.27]
21. In view of the various programmes envisaged by the BCI, the Committee desires
that it should approach the Ministry for the release of the grants allocated to it so that
the programmes proposed to be undertaken do not get derailed due to shortage of
funds. [Para 4.28]
22. The Committee takes note of the problems faced by Institute of Constitutional and
Parliamentary studies (ICPS) due to paucity of funds and accordingly, directs the Ministry to
release the funds allocated for the construction of building for the ICPS, so that the construction
work can be started. The Committee is, however, disappointed that huge surrenders of funds
recur in every financial year, starting form 2009-10. It, therefore, desires that the ICPS should
make all out efforts for utilization of allocated funds. [Para 4.31]
23. The Committee notes the infrastructural development works and the Diploma and
Certificate courses introduced by ILI and desires that more legal research activities should be
undertaken by the institute. [Para 4.34]
24. The Committee also takes note of the gaps between the demand projected and grants
received. Also the financial statements show that from 2009-10 onwards, every year, there has
been a surrender of funds. The Committee is of the view that such surrenders reflect the
tardy approach of the institute towards utilization of allocated funds. At the same time, the
Committee also recommends that the Department should also insure timely release of funds
so that the Institute is in a better position to utilize them. [Para 4.35]
25. The Committee is constrained to note that the grants earmarked for the construction
of ICADR building is pending with the Ministry, leading to undue delay in the construction of
building. From the last three financial years only a token amount of R1 lakh has been
allocated which has not been released. The Committee desires that the matter may be looked
into by the Department in consultation with the ICADR and necessary steps be taken for the
immediate release of funds to the ICADR. [Para 4.40]
26. To the query of the Committee, the representatives of ICADR submitted that the
Centre at New Delhi charges. R2500/- for one session of arbitration/conciliation which is very
nominal as compared to the amount charged by the private bodies in that field. The Committee
is unhappy that in spite of the Centre at New Delhi having nominal charges, it has not been
optimally used for arbitration/conciliation purpose by the parties. The Committee therefore,
desires that the facility offered by the Government at nominal charges should be popularized
so that private parties can be attracted to use it for arbitration/conciliation purpose. [Para 4.41]
27. The Committee takes note of the activities being taken up by the Official Language
Wing (OLW). The Committee feels that the OLW should also get translated the Bills/Acts in
more regional languages so that these can be used at the lower/subordinate level courts, where
the litigation work in done in regional languages. [Para 5.7]
28. The Committee takes note of the increase in the overall Budgetary allocation to the
Legislative Department. The Committee appreciates the austerity measures undertaken by the
Department following the directives of the Finance Ministry. The Committee suggests that the

58
VSP should upgrade on the quality of its publications in terms of layout, content and context.
It should also explore scope of bringing out e-books and e-publications. In Committee’s view,
active engagement of States in the promotion and publicity of its literature available in Hindi
by holding frequent competitions, seminars and conferences for school/college going students,
through the respective States, may increase the distribution of its books and journals among
more people. [Para 5.8]
29. The Committee appreciates the work undertaken by the Department during the last
financial year. The Committee takes note of the shortage of drafting personnel at various
levels. The Committee takes serious note of the shortage of drafting personnel as submitted
to it and urges the Department to coordinate with the Institute of Legislature Drafting and
Research (ILDR) in this regard for creation of a strong pool of experts in legislative drafting
from where it can draw it’s requirement. It is also of the considered view that the quality of
drafting of legislations should not be compromised at any cost and therefore, such an
important Department should be allowed to increase its strength so that the quality of
legislations drafted may not be affected. [Para 5.12]
30. A good fourteen years has gone by since the establishment of the ILDR in January,
1989. In this context, the Committee its constraint to note that a mere 24 Basic Courses of
three months duration each and 14 Appreciation Courses of fifteen days duration each has
been conducted in these fourteen years. The Committee is of the opinion that the institute has
not performed to its optimum. In this context, the Committee wishes to refer to the oral
submission of Secretary, Legislative Department stating that there is urgent need for augmenting
the Department’s personnel for legislative drafting which reflects the urgency of requirement
of skilled manpower. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the ILDR should frame
target of conducting a minimum of two Basic Courses and two Appreciation Courses each
financial year in view of the importance and necessity of having a strong pool of experts in
legislative drafting. [Para 5.13]
31. The Committee has also been continuously reminding the Department to expedite the
process of acquiring of land and construction of building for ILDR. However, the Committee
is again disappointed to note that only a token amount of R1 lakh has been allocated to ILDR
in BE 2013-14. The Committee believes that an institution of such a stature needs to have its
own building to carry out its functions. [Para 5.14]
32. The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Department in facilitating the
voting right to Non-resident citizens of India and also the simplification of the process of
submission of application for registration. However, the Committee feels that these few
thousands registrations need to be increased to justify the voting rights that has been
conferred on the NRIs. The Committee recommends the Government to take more initiatives
in this regard. [Para 5.18]
33. Family Courts are important instrument to reduce the pendency of cases. Under
Section 3(1)(a) of the Family Courts Act, 1984 it is mandatory for the State Governments to
set up a Family Court for every area in the State comprising a city or a town whose population
exceeds one million. In other areas of the States, the Family Courts may be set up if the State
Governments deem it necessary. However, the Committee is not satisfied with the slow pace
of establishment of Family Courts in different parts of the country even after two decades of
the enactment of the Family Court Act, 1984. The Committee is given to understand that lack
of finances is one of the main cause for slow pace of setting up of Family Courts. There is
perhaps a persistent demand from the States for higher assistance for setting up such Courts

59
both for meeting the expenditure for establishing such Courts and also for meeting the cost
for running them. The Committee impress upon the Ministry of Law & Justice to review the
funding pattern so that more Family Courts are set up. [Para 6.11]
34. The Committee reiterates its view expressed in its earlier Reports that, the Ministry
should envisage setting up of maximum number of Family Courts across the length and
breadth of the country and continuously pursue with the State Governments to come forward
in setting of the family courts to meet the objective of Family Courts Act, 1984. The
Committee is optimistic that the Family Courts can meaningfully keep in sharing the work
pressure on the Subordinate Judiciary. [Para 6.12]
35. The Committee takes note of the information given by the Director, National Judicial
Academy. The Committee is unhappy to note that NJA could not utilize its duly allocated funds
and the purpose behind the enhanced allocation for the succeeding years was thus not fulfilled.
The Committee desires that NJA should make optimum utilization of funds allocated to it. The
Committee urges the Ministry to work in close coordination with NJA to ensure that the
allocated funds for the year 2013-14 are utilized and the procedural impediments are not
allowed to obstruct the process. [Para 6.17]
36. The Committee commends the work of the Department in reducing the number of
pending Utilisation Certificates (UCs) from State Governments, as informed by Department of
Justice to the Committee that out of R1245.35 crores released between 1993-94 to 2010-11,
UCs of only R31.84 crores are pending. The Committee desires that the pending UCs be
obtained from the concerned States/UTs so that further Grants-in-aid may be released on time.
[Para 6.24]
37. The Committee takes note of the fact that infrastructure development for judiciary
represents a major component of the plan outlay of the Department of Justice in BE 2013-14
and the programme is in operation as a Centrally sponsored Scheme since 1993-94. The
Committee is however, constrained to mind that certain States have not been able to take full
advantage of the Scheme and as a result, they have been able to draw comparatively lesser
funds. The Committee further notes that there are certain States which were not able to draw
funds under the Scheme consecutively for one or more years. The Committee is unable to
understand the reasons why certain States have not been able to take the benefit of the
Scheme, which is so much tilted in their favour. Further, the Scheme is in operation since
1993-94 and large funds of the Central Government are being spent under the Scheme in the
form of assistance to States for improvement of infrastructure for dispensation of justice by
them. Keeping these factors in view, the Committee feels that its high time for the Department
of Justice to going for a review/audit of the said Scheme so as to ascertain on both these
aspects namely (i) the uneven and irregular drawl/utilization of funds by certain States and
(ii) the actual development in infrastructure that have taken place in the States and the extent
to which this has helped in speeding up the trial of cases. The committee is, however, happy
to note that the Ministry has sought the willingness of the ILI for evaluation of this scheme.
The Committee recommends expeditious action in the matter. [Para 6.25]
38. The Committee deeply appreciates the initiative of the Department of Justice by
bringing about a National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms in June, 2011. The
Committee notes that some allocations are made for certain activities under this Mission in
the BE 2012-13 but, the work could not take off and no expenditure took place under the
Mission during the year 2012-13. The Committee finds some modest allocations for different
activities under the Scheme in BE 2013-14. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would take
action seriously under the National Mission, which visualizes a vast and laudable objective of

60
ensuring to people, including the marginalized sections of the Society prompt and quality
service. [Para 6.29]
39. The Committee is more than convinced that speedy and efficient dispensation of justice
is the need of the country today and for meeting this objective, the fast track Courts can play
a major constructive role. With the Central assistance of 75% (90% in case of North Eastern
States), the Committee does not foresee any hesitation on the part of the States to set up such
fast track Courts for speedy trial in serious crimes against society including those involving
children, the elderly or the vulnerable sections of the Society. The Committee is convinced that
in case we succeed in curtailing the trial period in the Courts, a definite message would go
in the Society creating a feeling in the mind of the common man to abide by the laws due
to the fear of being punished. Such a scenario in Committee’s view would help in bringing
down the rate of crime in the country. The Committee accordingly, recommends that the
Department of Justice should take all possible steps to ensure that the fast track Courts are
set up in appropriate situations in the States and the States do not face impediments in this
regard. [Para 6.30]
40. The Committee takes notes of the serious activities envisaged under the tentative
Action Plan of the National Mission. In Committee’s view, the various actions enumerated in
the Action Plan are complimentary and supplementary to each other and would definitely prove
to be helpful in not only in speeding up the disposal of cases but also enhancing the quality
of their disposal. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should work on the Action
Plan in all seriousness and at the right earnest so that there is considerable progress of action
in the financial year ahead. The Committee however, reiterates its recommendations on the
last year’s Demand for Grants that the Ministry should determine definite time lines and
targets for the implementation of the Mission and put in place an effective monitoring also.
[Para 6.33]
41. The Committee is happy note that an allocation of R5 crore has been made for Action
Research and Studies under Judicial Reforms. The Committee is in agreement with the view
of the Ministry that the Scheme be implemented on a continuing basis through the Twelfth
Five Year Plan as an activity under the National Mission. The Committee hopes that the
implementation of the Scheme would definitely enhance the capabilities of all those involved
in the dispensation of justice including the mediators and conciliators and speed up the disposal
of cases. [Para 6.36]
42. The Committee is highly appreciative of this ambitious initiative of the Ministry to set
up Model Subordinate Courts at selected places in the country on a pilot basis. The Committee
takes note that these Courts, set up under the pilot project would be a model in various
respects from the point of view of convenience of all concerned, efficiency and quality of
justice. The Committee is happy to take note of the allocation of R26 crore for this purpose
for the year 2013-14. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would take action in this matter
in their right earnest. [Para 6.40]
43. The Committee is optimistic that the setting up of Model Courts will result in higher
productivity in terms of reduced time lines and timely justice dispensation. However, it is
appalled to note that no fund was released in 2012-13 out of the R7.50 crore allocation for
the Scheme. It, therefore, urges the Department of Justice to beef up its strategy in
releasing its proposals by assigning a strict time frame. The Committee, therefore, hopes to
be apprised of the progress made in this respect at the time of submitting the Action Taken
Replies. [Para 6.41]

61
44. The Committee takes note of the fact that for the financial year 2012-13, an amount
of R5 crore was allocated for implementation of Scheme in the North Eastern States and J&K
also. The Committee is constrained to note that Government have not been able to fully utilize
the budgetary allocations for the Scheme during the Eleventh Plan. Now, for the year 2013-14,
the allocations have been raised to R8 crore. The Committee reiterates its earlier
recommendations that Government should sincerely speed up action under the Scheme so as
to achieve the desired results. The Committee hopes that Government would take concrete
action in the coming financial year. [Para 6.45]
45. The Committee, even on previous occasions had shown concern on the effectiveness of
implementation of the project during the Eleventh Plan period when the Ministry had not been
able to exhaust the allocated funds all through. The Committee, however, appreciates the noble
objective of the project and it hopes that the Ministry would through proper monitoring and
coordination be able to achieve the desired results. [Para 6.50]
46. A perusal of expenditure pattern reveals that except for the year 2010-11, the ratio of
funds released vis-a-vis the BE was less than 50%. The Committee wonders that since this is
a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme, the Department of Justice should not have faced the
problem that it faces in case of other Schemes. In the last two years the position in releasing
the funds has further deteriorated. The Committee regrets to note that despite the concerns
expressed by it in the report on Demand for Grants for the year 2012-13, the release of funds
in that year had remained very low, i.e., R90 crores out of R213.66 crores. The Committee,
therefore, directs the Governments to check this trend and remove the bottlenecks, if any, in
this regard. [Para 6.54]
47. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry are in the process of implementing
Phase-II of the e-Courts Mission Mode Project. The Committee also takes note of the new
components added under Phase-II. The Committee hopes that the employment of IT in the
various fields associated with the functioning of the Courts, the advocates as well as the
litigants would go a long way in cutting on wasteful time and energy in the handling of
litigation work which is mostly handled manually at present.  [Para 6.58]
48. The Committee notes that no allocation has been made for the Phase-II of the Project
for the financial year 2013-14. Department has given justification that in view of the
Phase-I still in progress and slated to be completed only in March, 2014, the projection under
this component may be reflected from the financial year 2014-15. The Committee desires that
the Government may complete Phase-I as per the set Time-line so that Phase-II of the project
can be taken up without delay. [Para 6.59]
49.  ........ The Committee recommends that the Government should seriously examine the
feasibility of this proposal. [Para 6.60]
50. The Committee is happy to note that the Government has been sensitive towards the
lukewarm response from the State Governments for the setting up of Gram Nyayalayas and
a study has been carried out with reference to certain States for examining the effectiveness
of these Nyayalayas. The Committee hopes that the study undertaken by the Government
would definitely help in making necessary corrections and reinforcing the institution of Gram
Nyayalayas. In Committee’s view the initiative to have Gram Nyayalayas is a laudable one as
it is a useful link in making available justice at the door step and at a lesser cost. The
Committee hopes that the issues involved due to which there has been a reluctance on the
part of the States to have Gram Nyayalayas would be considered seriously by the Ministry and

62
all out efforts would be made to resolve them. The Committee also recommends the Ministry
to consider the feasibility of enhancing the Central assistance in order to motivate the States
to go in for the Gram Nyayalayas. [Para 6.65]
51. The Committee notes that the TFC had given a target of disposal of petty cases to the
tune of R225 lakhs per year and 75 lakhs cases by Lok Adalats in five years. By this
standards, the R20.57 lakhs cases cleared by Lok Adalats in 2012-13 is far from close to target.
The Committee also wishes to point out that the TFC had recommended a grant of  R5000
crore for the period 2010-15 out of which a mere R1425.23 crore has been released till
December 31,2012 which is not encouraging. Therefore, the Department of Justice should
review its performance in this respect and make holistic efforts to encourage States in setting
up of more shift Courts, Lok Adalats and ADR Centers to clear petty cases which are logging
the Courts. [Para 6.70]
52. The Committee is unhappy for the large number of vacancies that exist at present in the
Supreme Court and the High Courts in the country. The Committee is convinced that one of
the major factors for such large number of vacancies in the higher judiciary is the prevailing
system of selection of Judges for appointment in the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The
Committee reiterates its often stated view that the present system of appointment of Judges in
the higher judiciary calls for a review. The Committee accordingly, recommends the Government
to initiate action in the right earnest for reviewing the present system of filling up posts of
Judges in the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The Committee hopes that with Judges in
position in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts, the pendency of cases would lessen.
Incidentally, the Committee would also like to impress upon the judiciary to fill up the vacancies
of the clerical staff in the Supreme Court and the High Courts in the interest of efficiency by
reinforcing the secretarial support to the Judges. [Para 6.74]
53. The Committee is happy to note the proposal to have High Courts in the States of
Tripura, Manipur and Meghalaya. This, in Committee’s view would provide a much needed
relief to the persons belonging to these three States. This move would not only save on
litigant’s time and money but would also help in quicker disposal of cases. The Committee
would like the related modalities and procedures in the setting up of these High Courts to be
completed expeditiously. The Committee, in this context also strongly recommends that the
Circuit Bench of the Kolkata High Court at Siliguri should be made functional without any
further loss of time. [Para 6.75]
54. The Committee takes note of the justification furnished by the Supreme Court for
their projected demands. However, the details of expenses incurred under the different sub-
head of ‘Professional Services’ for the last three years may be furnished at the time of giving
Action Taken Replies. The Committee incidentally also observes in this context that the head
‘Professional Services’ be termed as ‘Security Services’ so as to reflect the correct nature of
the expenditure.  [Para 7.2]
55. The Committee feels that the unwillingness towards establishment of the other Benches
of the Supreme Court cannot be justified on the grounds that it would attract a cumbersome
process of Constitutional amendment and endanger national unity. The reply that Supreme
Court represents national symbol and a unifying force remains intact even if the benches of
the Supreme Court are set up as, several High Courts have benches and also, there are High
Courts which have jurisdiction over more than one State. The Committee strongly feels that
it does not play any divisive role in any way. The Committee, therefore reiterates its earlier
view for establishment of other Benches of Supreme Court of India in consonance with the
Article 130, Constitutional of India. [Para 7.4]

63
56. The Committee expresses its serious concern over the mounting of cases pending in
Supreme Court. In view of the submission made by the Registrar, Supreme Court to it, the
Committee urges the Government to conduct a comprehensive comparative study of the
working of the Supreme Court vis-à-vis the apex Courts of other countries in order to identify
the grey areas. Thereafter, the course of action to augment the institution may be laid down.
[Para 7.8]
57. The National Court Management System (NCMS) reports that India has one of the
largest judicial systems in the world, with over 3 crore of cases and sanctioned strength of
some 18,871 judges. The present judge to population ratio being 15.5 judges per million
population is grossly inadequate to dispense the justice in a reasonable time, which is also a
reason for the high pendency of cases. The Committee strongly recommends that the judge-
population ratio may be corrected by appointing more judges in Courts to reduce pendency and
ensure timely delivery of justice. In Committees view, timely delivery of justice would go a
long way in enforcing discipline in the society, improvement in the compliance of the laws and
consequently curbing in corruption in the society which is quite high on the Governments
agenda, today. [Para 7.9]

REPORT
The Readjustment of Representations of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in
Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Bill, 2013 ( Annexure-I ) is an Ordinance replacing
legislation introduced on the 26th February, 2013 in the Council of States. The Statement of
Objects and Reasons of the Bill outlines the basic objectives of the proposed legislation/Ordinance
and is reproduced below:–
“Articles 330 and 332 of the Constitution provide for reservation of seats for the Scheduled
Castes and the Scheduled Tribes respectively in the House of the People and in the Legislative
Assemblies of the States, in proportion to their population. Articles 82 and 170 of the
Constitution provide for readjustment of seats after each Census. Accordingly, the seats for the
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies
of the States have been readjusted as per Census 2001.
A Writ Petition (Civil) No. 540 of 2011, Virendra Pratap and another vs. Union of India and
others was filed in the Supreme Court contending that by virtue of the Scheduled Castes and
Scheduled Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act, 2002 (No.10 of 2003), several castes, which had
not been included in the list of Scheduled Tribes, were included as Scheduled Tribes and
despite such inclusion their representation in the Delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
Constituencies Order, 2008 was not done. The Supreme Court vide its judgment dated the
10th January, 2012 directed the Election Commission of India to consider the case of the
Scheduled Tribes which had been included in the list of the Scheduled Tribes by virtue of the
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act, 2002 (No. 10 of 2003) and
to take appropriate steps for their representation in the House of the People as well as in the
State Legislative Assembly. Pursuant thereto, the Election Commission desired that a legislation
may be enacted specifically empowering the Election Commission to carry out re-adjustment of
seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the light of the revised population
figures of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, as may be ascertained and estimated
by the Census Commissioner with reference to 1st March, 2001, after taking into account the
population figures of the castes and tribes which have been declared as the Scheduled Castes
and the Scheduled Tribes after publication of 2001 Census.
After the Census of 2001 and up to 31st May, 2012, several castes and tribes have been
included in and excluded from the lists of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes by eleven
Parliamentary Amendment Acts. Thus, there was an urgent need to review and restore the
statutory rights of those castes and tribes so included and excluded all over the country.
As the Parliament was not in session and immediate steps were required to be taken to
implement the aforesaid Judgment of the Supreme Court, the President was pleased to
promulgate the Readjustment of Representation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in
Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Ordinance, 2013 on the 30th January, 2013. The
Ordinance inter alia provided as follows—
(i) the Census Commissioner to ascertain and estimate the varied population figures of
the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the States as on the last Census held
in 2001 and to notify the same in the Gazette of India;
(ii) the Election Commission to make necessary amendments in the Delimitation of
Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Order, 2008 for the purpose of giving proper
representation to the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes in Lok Sabha and

2
Legislative Assemblies of the States by readjustment of Parliamentary and Legislative
Assemblies territorial Constituencies;
(iii) the Election Commission of India to cause publication of amendments made in the
existing Delimitation Order and dates of its operation;
(iv) the Election Commission to make necessary correction of the errors in the said
Delimitation Order and also to make necessary alterations therein, pursuant to any change
in boundaries and name of any district or territorial division.”
2. An Ordinance, namely, the Readjustment of Representation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
Tribes in Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Ordinance, 2013 was promulgated by Hon’ble
President of India on the 30th January, 2013 ( Annexure-II) which is liable to be repealed upon the
enactment of the proposed Legislation in terms of its Clause 10. The Committee takes note of the
Order of Supreme Court in the Writ Petition (Civil) No. 540 of 2011 in the matter of Virendra Pratap
and another vs. Union of India and others wherein the Election Commission of India has been directed
to take appropriate steps for representation of Scheduled Tribes in the Lower House in Parliament as
well as in the State Assembly in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution for due
representation of Scheduled Tribes population in the State of Uttar Pradesh. Following the judgement
of Supreme Court, the Election Commission of India had expressed its inability to Government to
carry out the Orders of the Supreme Court as it did not have the power to do so under existing laws.
Accordingly, the Election Commission requested the Government to enact necessary legislation to
enable it to carry out the directions of Supreme Court. The Government while examining the
judgement of Supreme Court noted that the judgement was only applicable in respect of the State of
Uttar Pradesh whereas several castes and tribes have been included and/or excluded from the list of
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes under Articles 341 and 342 of Constitution respectively, in
almost all the States across the country through several amendments effected to Scheduled Caste and
Scheduled Tribe Orders after the 2001 census. The Committee has been apprised that as many as
eleven amendments after 2001 census till 31st May, 2012 have been passed which need to be
accounted for necessitating readjustment of seats meant for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
in the Lower House of Parliament and the State Legislature Assemblies. The necessity of proposed
legislation is essentially to enable the Registrar General of India to estimate and ascertain the varied
population figures of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in relation to the 2001 census and to
empower the Election Commission of India to carry out readjustment of Parliamentary and Assembly
seats on the basis of revised population figures of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
3. Clause 4 of the Bill empowers the Election Commission to carry out amendments as may be
necessary in the Delimitation Order, 2008 by readjustment of territorial constituencies of States and
UTs for Lok Sabha and the Legislative Assemblies having regard to Articles 81, 170, 330 and 332 of
the Constitution and Section 8 of Delimitation Act, 2002. These amendments when done, would be
deemed to have taken place in First and Second Schedules to the Representation of the People
Act, 1950 which reflects allocation of seats in the House of People and Legislative Assemblies. In
order to carry out readjustment of Parliamentary Constituencies the Registrar of General and Census
Commission of India would provide revised figure of population of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
Tribes up to 31st May, 2012 to the Election Commission of India for the purpose. The date of
commencement of the Act would be from the date of Promulgation of the Ordinance i.e. 30th January,
2013 in terms of Clause 1 of the Bill. The Provisions of Bill would be applicable retrospectively
because the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India has already started ascertaining the
figure of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes during the period following 2001 Census till 31st
May, 2012, starting with the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Registrar General of India have already
notified total population figure of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and percentage of their
population with reference to the total population of the State of Uttar Pradesh as on 1st April, 2013

3
in Gazette of India ( Annexure-III). It is noted from the figures that the percentage of Scheduled
Tribe population is 0.4 per cent of the State population and this has no representation in the
Parliamentary as well as Assembly Constituencies of that State. After the enactment of this legislation,
the Election Commission is supposed to carry out necessary alterations in the Delimitation Order, 2008
to give due representation to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to total population
figure in the Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies of States and Union Territories.
4. The Bill empowers the Election Commission to carry out readjustment of Parliamentary and
Assembly Constituencies on the basis of revised Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes percentage
vis-a-vis the total population of State/UT. However, the Secretary, Legislative Department during his
deposition before the Committee referred to the precedent of 1976 when readjustment of Parliamentary
and Assembly Constituencies took place following inclusion/exclusion of certain Castes and Tribes in
the list under Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Order (Amendment) Act, 1976.
5. The Secretariat issued a press communiqué inviting writing suggestions from the Members of
public on 25th March, 2013. The written memoranda numbering 21 received from the public,
including some public representatives, were forwarded to the Legislative Department of Government
of India for their comments. A Statement showing the issues raised in these Memoranda/representations
and the comments of the Legislative Department thereon is enclosed (Annexure-IV).
6. The Secretary, Legislative Department, Government of India in his disposition before the
Committee on 5th April, 2013 apprised the Committee that Hon’ble High Court of Bombay at Goa in
its judgement dated the 11th February, 2013 on Writ Petition No. 230/2007 regarding Goa State
Scheduled Tribes Action Committee Vs. State of Goa and others had directed the Election Commission
of India to decide the representation of Scheduled Tribes in the Lower House of Parliament and State
Legislative Assemblies within a period of eight months. The Bombay High Court while pronouncing
the aforesaid judgement made reference to the Supreme Court judgement in Virendra Pratap case.
7.  The Committee notes that as per the Constitution of India, readjustment and delimitation of
constituencies both Parliamentary and Assembly are to be done after every decennial census in terms
of Articles 82 and 170 of Constitution. The Delimitation Commission was constituted four times in the
past in the history of independent India, i.e., in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002. The delimitation initiated
in 2002 was done without changing the overall seats of Parliamentary Constituencies and Assembly
Constituencies of different States and it got completed in 2008. However, the delimitation carried out
in 2008 did not take into account the variation in the population of SC/ST during the period following
1st March, 2001. A Statement giving the State/UT wise population as per 2001 census and the
representation (% wise) of SC/ST therein is enclosed (Annexure-V).
8. The population figures in respect of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are under revision
by the office of Registrar General of India and would be available to public at the end of this year
as reported by the Registrar General of India to the Committee on the 5th of April, 2013. The
Committee was informed that the population figure of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in
percentage terms with reference to the total population figure had increased from 14.6 per cent in
1971 census to 16.2 per cent in 2001 Census. Similarly, the population figure of Scheduled Tribes
had increased from 6.9 per cent in 1971 Census to 8.2 per cent in 2001 census. The overall increase
of population figure of SC and ST in 2001 Census has led the Delimitation Commission to increase
the seats for Scheduled Castes in Lok Sabha from 79 to 84 and for Scheduled Tribes from 41 to 47.
9. Statements giving statistics of Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies, including these
reserved for SC/ST on the basis of the delimitation exercises of 1976 and 2008 are enclosed
(Annexures-VI & VII) .
10. The Secretary in his deposition apprised the Committee that the Bill is not meant for
delimitation of Constituencies but it has a limited mandate of giving representation to Scheduled Castes

4
and Scheduled Tribes in view of constitutional provisions enshrined under Articles 330 and 332 of
Constitution. The legislation will enable the Office of Registrar General to ascertain an estimate the
varied population figure of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes with reference to 2001 census
where after the Election Commission of India would be carrying out necessary alteration in the
Delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Order, 2008. To the query of the Committee
whether the readjustment of the constituencies can be reviewed, the Secretary submitted that the
Delimitation Commission which was constituted in 2002 has become functus officio after 2008.
Therefore, the Election Commission of India and State Election Commissions which were part of the
Delimitation Commission would be entrusted the task of readjustment of seats of Parliament and
Assembly Constituencies after the enactment of this legislation. Another query was raised whether
readjustment of seats Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies would lead to limited delimitation of
reserved constituencies or its adjoining constituencies, the Secretary submitted that there may be
limited change of boundary of Parliamentary or Assembly Constituencies and also change in boundary
and name of any district or territorial division in order to give effect to readjustment of seats under
the Bill.
11. Some Members, during the course of the deliberations of the Bill, pointed out that the
exercise for the Election Commission would turn out to be a major one. However, in Committee’s
view, this exercise is limited to provide for the readjustment of representation of Parliamentary
and Assembly constituencies in so far as such readjustment is necessitated by inclusion in or
exclusion of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes by the Parliamentary Acts after
the 2001 Census and upto 31st May, 2012 broadly on the lines of the Scheduled Castes and
Scheduled Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act, 1976 (108 of 1976). This exercise would only result
in increase or decrease of a few reserved seats of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It
will neither change the number of constituencies nor will it be a delimitation exercise.
12. Further, Members also wanted to know as to why the task could not be entrusted to
the Delimitation Commission. In this connection, the Committee observes that the Delimitation
Commission constituted under the Delimitation Commission ceased to exist w.e.f. 1st June,
2008 on completion of its task of delimitating the constituencies throughout the country. Thus,
entrusting this task to the Delimitation Commission would require constituting the Commission
afresh.  The Delimitation Commission is meant to delimit the constituencies throughout the
country which is a mammoth exercise. The present task of readjustment of representation of
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies is only
a limited exercise. Therefore, any fresh Delimitation Commission does not seem to be
appropriate. Under similar circumstances in the year 1976 this exercise was entrusted to the
Election Commission of India under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Orders
(Amendment) Act, 1976 (108 of 1976).
13. There was another query raised by some Members that the judgement, based on which
the present Bill has been drafted, pertained to Uttar Pradesh only. That being the case, it was
not proper to cover other parts of the country to have delimitation done throughout the
country with regard to SC/ST communities. The Committee, however, notes that limiting the
present delimitation exercise to the Uttar Pradesh only would be violative of right to equality.
Once a judgement is pronounced on any particular issue then principle laid down in it has to
be uniformly applied to all States. There is an identical Writ Petition, namely, W.P. No. 230
of 2007 filed before the Hon’ble High Court of Bombay at Goa wherein reservation of seats
for the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of Goa was sought. The Hon’ble High
Court in its judgement dated the 4th February, 2013 has directed the Election Commission that
the representation of the petitioner seeking reservation of the Scheduled Tribes in the
Legislative Assembly of Goa may be decided as expeditiously as possible and in any case within
a period of eight months. Therefore, this exercise has to be done in all the States.

5
14. In principle, the Committee agrees to the provisions of the Bill. The Bill seeks to
recognize the rights of the persons belonging to SC/ST communities in the matter of their
representation in the Parliament and the State Assemblies in terms of the provisions of the
Constitution and the legislation on the subject. However, the Committee desires that the
Election Commission of India and other related Agencies should take all care to give effect
to the provisions of the Bill in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Bill.
15. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed.

MINUTES OF DISSENT SUBMITTED BY – SHRI SUKHENDU SEKHAR ROY, M.P.
(RAJYA SABHA)
Please refer to the verbatim records of the proceedings of the meetings of the Committee held
on 5th and 12th April, 2013 in the above-mentioned subject and the points raised/submissions made
by the Hon’ble Members on the Bill referred to above. In the last meeting, i.e. on 12th April, 2013
the members were given to understand that many meetings would further be held and views of experts
would be sought for in the matter, as would be evident from the last few lines at page 29 of the said
recordings. However, it is not known whether any expert view was obtained in the matter as no copy
of the expert view, if any, has been circulated among the members, it is, therefore, not understood
what prompted the Chairman to convene today’s meeting for “adoption” of a draft report without
having further discussions and obtaining expert view in the matter as assured in the last meeting.
Without prejudice to what have been stated hereinabove but fully relying upon them and in
exercise of my right to dissent, I oppose adoption of the Draft Report on the following, amongst
other, grounds:
1. The Draft Report (hereinafter called ‘DR’) which refers to Article 170 of the Constitution
for readjustment of the seats for SC & ST is the guiding factor for any such readjustment.
However, no power for readjustment of seats after each census has been vested to the
Election Commission of India under Article 324 of the Constitution and/or any other
statute/rules governing such readjustment. On the contrary Article 82 inter alia  stipulates
that territorial constituencies shall be readjusted “by such authority and in such manner
as Parliament may by law determine”. In pursuance of Article 82 of the Constitution,
Parliament has since passed The Delimitation Act, 2002 (Act 33 of 2002) for constitution
of Delimitation Commission and empowering it for readjustment of the allocation of seats
in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies in the State and “for matter
connected therewith”. Section 8 of the Delimitation Commission inter alia  envisages that
the Commission shall, having regard to the provision of 81, 170, 330 and 332, shall
determine the number of seats to be reserved for SC/ST and publish its orders to that
effect after considering all objections and suggestions and holding public sittings at such
place of places in each State as it thinks fit. Therefore, the powers of readjustment of
seats, which forms part of delimitation falls within the jurisdiction of the Delimitation
Commission, which cannot be taken away or usurped by any other authority, not to speak
of the Election Commission of India.
The Judgment referred to in the DR under reference has no applicability in the present
case inasmuch as the said judgment was exclusively meant for disposing of that particular
case before the Court and the ratio of judgment is per incuriam and not per curiam. That
the Government Promulgated an Ordinance on 30th January, 2013 as, according to the
D.R., the Parliament was not in session and the immediate steps were required to be
taken to implement the aforesaid judgment of the Supreme Court, such reasons must be
considered as concocted, baseless and unacceptable in as such as the Supreme judgment
was passed in 2011 and the Ordinance was promulgated in January, 2013. In between the
period there had been a series of Parliament sessions and the Government did not initiate
any action for about 2 years because the Government was also aware that the aforesaid
judgment was not meant for readjustment of SC/ST seats all over the country. Moreover,
it was not mentioned by the Government/Election Commission that it was the Delimitation
9

10
Commission under the Delimitation Act which is empowered to make the readjustments,
and not the Election Commission of India or for that matter any other authority. The
Judgment of the Bombay High Court 4.2.13 is also limited only to the Petitioner(s)
concerned and does not ask for countrywide readjustment of the seats for SC/ST.
Had the Government good and clear intention for taking legal steps for readjustment
of representation of SC/ST the following measures ought to have been effected in the
meantime.
(a) Directing the Census Commissioner to ascertain and estimate the varied
population figures of SC/ST (Election Commission deposed before the
committee saying that it was not known when the figures would be made
available by the Census Commission – a complete uncertainty prevails in the
respect).
(b) Reconstituting the Delimitation Commission under Sec. 3 of the Delimitation
Act 2002 and causing a notice to be published to that effect.
(c) All figures of SC/ST ought to have been published and views of respective
States and such other representative bodies/organizations of the SC/ST should
have been taken and considered by holding public sitting too.
(d) Directing the Delimitation Commission to reconstitute to cause publication of
amendment of SC/ST seats within a definite Time.
In the DR, a reference has been drawn citing a precedent whereby the Election Commission
was authorized for readjustment of seats in 1976. However, bad precedent does not hold good to
subserve the greater interest of the SC/ST communities, particularly of an era ante, notoriously known
as Emergency Period when even the fundamental rights of the citizens and freedom of Press were
abridged/taken away and the citizens were compelled to abide by all draconian measures and mandates
issued at the whims and fancies of the ruling party Government.
In fine, it appears from each and every line of the proposed Bill that it seeks to empower the
Election Commission of India to usrupt all the existing powers of the Delimitation Commission, for
the purpose of the present Bill, although Article 324 of the Constitution of India envisages inter alia
that “the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral roll and all elections to
Parliament and State Legislature………shall be vested in the Commission (election commission)”.
Therefore, without reconstituting the Delimitation Commission but preparing the present Bill instead,
the Government seeks to take away the powers of the Delimitation Commission and to give all such
powers to Election Commission for collateral and/or oblique purposes which is out and out unconstitutional
and not acceptable both in the context and form of the proposed Bill.
In view of what have been stated hereinabove, I vehemently oppose the adoption of the Draft
Report and/or endorsement of the proposed Bill to its hilt and suggest for more deliberations on the
subject after taking views of the constitutional experts and the views of all concerned States/Union
Territories.

3. Following were the major views/suggestions expressed by the Members of the Committee:–
• In Principle, the objective of the legislation, i.e., to give representation to the SC/ST (on
the basis of updated status) in the Parliamentary/Assembly constituencies is acceptable
• Readjustment is a part of delimitation. While going for readjustment, limited delimitation
of constituencies might be required. This function should not be vested with the Election
Commission of India as it is not the primary function of Election Commission under
Article 324 of the Constitution whereas delimitation is explicitly under Article 327 of
Constitution.
• During 2002 and May 2013 as many as 550 Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes were
included and 74 Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes excluded through 11 notifications
of the Government. It is a stupendous task for the Election Commission to give representation
to these castes/tribes in the Parliament and Assembly Constituencies. This job should have
ideally been entrusted  to the Delimitation Commission.
• The Supreme Court’s decision on the Writ Petition (Civil) No. 540 of 2011 in Virender
Pratap and another Vs. Union of India and others, mentioned in the Statement of Objects
and Reasons appended to the Bill,  is not a judgment of the Apex court. Rather it is an
order of general kind passed by that Court on the eve of 2012 Assembly election of the
State of Uttar Pradesh and is limited to the prayer in writ petition and giving representation
to Scheduled Tribe in a particular State.  But, the proposed legislation is attempting to give
representation to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled T ribes in Lok Sabha and Assembly
Constituencies in the whole country. The Government took the route of ordinance almost
after one year to enact a law to give right to Election Commission to readjust the
constituencies which is constitutionally not the mandate of that body.
• The exercise of promulgation of ordinance and introduction of Bill replacing that ordinance
is an attempt on the part of the Government to appropriate the power of delimitation of
constituencies of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies in the name of giving representation to
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes through the Election Commission of India.
• An anomalous situation was pointed out where one of the castes in State of the UP was
declared as Scheduled Caste as well as Scheduled Tribe. While giving representation to
these castes, the Delimitation Commission headed by a judicial officer can adjudicate the
matter but this cannot not done by the Election Commission on the basis of majority of
votes.
• The Delimitation Act, 2002 has not been repealed but the Delimitation Commission has
become functus officio  after 2008 as a result of which the Election Commission is being
vested with the power once conferred upon the Delimitation Commission through the

18
proposed legislation which is improper. The better course of action is that the Delimitation
Commission which is an adjudicative body can be revived to carry out readjustment of
seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as well as limited delimitation/readjustment
of seats as an effect thereto.
• Since the matter involves the readjustment of seats of Legislative Assemblies of State and
Union Territories the State and Union Territories should be consulted in the matter before
passing this legislation.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
Articles 330 and 332 of the Constitution provide for reservation
of seats for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes respectively
in the House of the People and in the Legislative Assemblies of the
States, in proportion to their population. Articles 82 and 170 of the
Constitution provide for readjustment of seats after each Census.
Accordingly, the seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies of the States
have been readjusted as per Census 2001.
2. A Writ Petition (Civil) No. 540 of 2011, Virendra Pratap and
another vs. Union of India and others was filed in the Supreme Court
contending that by virtue of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act, 2002 (No.10 of 2003), several castes,
which had not been included in the list of Scheduled Tribes, were
included as Scheduled Tribes and despite such inclusion their
representation in the Delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
Constituencies Order, 2008 was not done. The Supreme Court vide its
judgment dated the 10th January, 2012 directed the Election Commission
of India to consider the case of the Scheduled Tribes which had been
included in the list of the Scheduled Tribes by virtue of the Scheduled
Castes and Scheduled Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act, 2002 (No. 10
of 2003) and to take appropriate steps for their representation in the
House of the People as well as in the State Legislative Assembly.
Pursuant thereto, the Election Commission desired that a legislation
may be enacted specifically empowering the Election Commission to
carry out re-adjustment of seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
Tribes in the light of the revised population figures of the Scheduled
Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, as may be ascertained and estimated
by the Census Commissioner with reference to 1st March, 2001, after
taking into account the population figures of the castes and tribes
which have been declared as the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled
Tribes after publication of 2001 Census.
3. After the Census of 2001 and up to 31st May, 2012, several
castes and tribes have been included in and excluded from the lists of
the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes by eleven Parliamentary
Amendment Acts. Thus, there was an urgent need to review and
restore the statutory rights of those castes and tribes so included and
excluded all over the country.
4. As the Parliament was not in session and immediate steps
were required to be taken to implement the aforesaid Judgment of the
Supreme Court, the President was pleased to promulgate the
Readjustment of Representation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
Tribes in Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Ordinance, 2013

29
on the 30th January, 2013. The Ordinance inter alia provided as
follows—
(i) the Census Commissioner to ascertain and estimate
the varied population figures of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled
Tribes in the States as on the last Census held in 2001 and to notify
the same in the Gazette of India;
(ii) the Election Commission to make necessary amendments in
the Delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies Order,
2008 for the purpose of giving proper representation to the Scheduled
Castes or the Scheduled Tribes in Lo k Sabha and Legislative Assemblies
of the States by readjustment of Parliamentary and Legislative Assemblies
territorial constituencies;
(iii) the Election Commission of India to cause publication of
amendments made in the existing Delimitation Order and dates of its
operation;
(iv) the Election Commission to make necessary correction of
the errors in the said Delimitation Order and also to make necessary
alterations therein, pursuant to any change in boundaries and name of
any district or territorial division.
5. The Bill seeks to replace the aforesaid Ordinance.

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 7 of the Bill confers powers upon the
Election Commission to make, by notification, correction of printing
mistake or any error in the Delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
Constituencies Order, 2008 and also to make necessary amendments
therein, pursuant to any change in boundaries and name of any district
or territorial division.
2. Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 9 of the Bill confers powers upon
the Central Government to issue orders to remove any difficulty which
may arise to give effect to the provisions of the proposed enactment
within a period of two years.
3. The notification issued by the Election Commission shall be
laid, as soon as, it is issued, before each House of Parliament and
before the Legislative Assembly of the State concerned. The order
made by the Central Government shall be laid, as soon as, it is issued,
before each House of Parliament.
4. The matters in respect of which the notification may be
issued or the order may be made are matters of procedure and
administrative detail. The delegation of legislative power is, therefore,
of a normal character.

 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, 
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on 
its behalf, do hereby present this Sixth Report on  Demands for Grants (2005-06) pertaining to the 
Ministry of Law and Justice. 
2. The Committee heard the concerne d officers of the Ministry in its sittings held on 30 and 31 
March, 2005. 
3. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied upon the  
following:----- 
 (i) Presentations made by the concerned officers of the Ministry;  
 (ii) Detailed Demands for Grants of  the Ministry for the year 2005-06;  
 (iii) Explanatory Note on the Demands for Grants (2005-06) received from the Ministry;

Hundred First Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs on the Demands for Grants (2003- 04) of the Ministry;  
 (vi) Written replies furnished by the Ministry to the Questionnaires sent to it by the 
Secretariat; and  
 (vii) Written clarifications to the points/issues raised by the Members in the meetings of the 
Committee. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on 11th April, 2005.

Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

DELIMITATION COMMISSION 
6.1. On a specific query raised about the progress of delimitation work, the Department submitted 
the following reply :- 
 The Delimitation Commission was constituted in July, 2002. It became functional in 
November/December, 2002. The Commission ---- in terms of the Constitutional provision ----- 
was to delimit the constituencies on the basis of 1991 census figures. By June, 2003 the 
Commission had completed almost 60 per cent of its work. The totality of the Commission’s 
work (all the Parliamentary constituencies and the Assembly constituencies in all the states in 
the country) would have been completed by November/December, 2003. But it could not be 
done because the Parliament amended the Constitution by the Constitution (Eighty-Seventh 
Amendment) Act, 2003, which provides that the delimitation work shall be done by the 
Commission on the basis of the 2001 census and not the 1991 census figures. As a 
consequence, the work done by the Commission on the basis of the 1991 census became non-
est by the operation of law. The Commission, however, started preliminary work on the basis of 
the provisional 2001 census figures, which were available. But the preliminary work could not 
be taken to the logical extent because, even the provisional 2001 census figures regarding the 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes were not available. 
 The 2001 Census figures for most of the States were published on December 31, 2003. 
Thereafter the Commission took-up the work of collecting data and tabulating the same. While 
the process was going on the Lok Sabha was dissolved and fresh elections were declared. The 
Commission has five Lok Sabha Members from each State as its associate members. Where the 
number of M.Ps in a State is less than five, all of them become Commission’s members. With 
the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the associate members ceased to be members by operation of 
law. Even otherwise during the elections, the fieldwork by the Commission was almost 
stopped. After the constitution of the Fourteenth Lok Sabha the Commission requested Hon’ble 
Speaker to nominate associate members to the Delimitation Commission from each State. After 
receipt of the nominations the Commission restarted the delimitation work which is progressing 
on a tight schedule. 
 The delimitation of the Lok Sabha and assembly  constituencies in all the States is a time 
consuming work. Under the scheme of the Act asso ciate members are to be associated with the 
delimitation work from the very beginning. As a consequence there have to be more than one 
meeting with the associate members from each State. Thereafter, the draft delimitation 
proposals are published in newspapers and suggestions and views are invited from the public. 
Finally, the public meetings are held by the Commission in all the States and the draft finalized, 
after that. 
 Delimitation work in all the States in the country is at different stages. Four States viz; 
Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal and the Union Territory of Pondicherry are 
scheduled to go to polls in May, 2006. Out of these, Final Delimitation Order has been issued in 
respect of Pondicherry and published in the State and Central Gazette on 31.3.2005. For Kerala 
Public Hearings have been scheduled in the last week of April and Final Order is expected to be 

issued in the first week of May. Final Order in respect of the other three States will be issued 
after completion of the Delimitation exercise which is at an advanced stage. 
 It may be added that under Article 82 of the Constitution, the readjustment of 
constituencies for the House of the People “shall take effect from such date as the President 
may, by order, specify”. Similarly under Article 170 (3) of the Constitution, the readjustment of 
constituencies for the State Legislative Assemblies “shall take effect from such date as the 
President may, by order, specify”. The question of  elections to be held on the basis of the new 
delimitation exercise will be dependent on the date determined by the President of India. 
6.2 The Committee impresses upon the Delimitati on Commission to expedite the delimitation 
exercise in the Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies in al l the States, particularly the 
delimitation of assembly constituencies which should be completed we ll in advance in those 
States which are scheduled to go to polls in M ay, 2006. As regards th e readjustment of the 
constituencies of the House of People, which shall take effect from the date to be specified by the 
President, the Committee impresses upon the Legisl ative Department to ta ke timely action for 
issue of Presidential Notification.

Some Connected  Issues 
REVISION OF ELECTORAL ROLLS 
7.31 The electoral rolls are revised by the Election Commission every year. All persons who attain 
18 years of age or above are eligible for inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls and can apply 
for the same. Budget Estimates for 2005-06 for meeting expenses on revision of electoral rolls are 
covered under sub-head 00.103. 

7.32 Some members raised the issue of revision of electoral rolls in different Parliamentary as 
well as the Assemblies Constituencies. It was observed that there had been numerous complaints 
of the voters all over the country about irregular ities committed in preparation of these rolls. 
Generally, persons employed in Government establishments are drawn to undertake the job 
whose lack of professionalism leave many lac unae. This ultimately impedes the successful 
implementation of the scheme. The Committee, is, therefore, of the view that to overcome such 
shortcomings, the Election Commission should cons ider establishing its offices for this purpose 
at district levels. It would not only cover the maximum voters who are not otherwise included in 
the rolls but also ensure great er accountability towards the lapses . It further feels that some 
parts of the country, strategically located, lik e North Eastern States and Jammu and Kashmir 
need to be covered under the scheme by launching vigorous campaigning in this field.

7.33 Non-Plan Budget Estimates fo r the year 2005-06 for Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) has

Commission, however, is working out a detailed plan for upgradation of Electronic Voting Machines

phasing out of EVMs over the next few years based on the age of the machine and the lifespan of its

7.34 The Committee has been informed that some State Election Commissioners have been 
requesting to provide them with EVMs for conduct of elections to local bodies. The Election 
Commission has convened a meeting of all State Election Commissioners at Hyderabad on 18th April, 
2005 in which the issue of utilization of EVMs in local bodies will be discussed and a view taken 
thereafter. The issue of procurement of additional machines to augment the present stock from funds 
to be made available by the State Election Commissions/State Governments will also be one of the 
items for discussion and decision. 
7.35 The Committee feels that being one of the largest democracies of the world, Government’s 
constant endeavor should be directed to ensure th at elections are held in free and fair manner. 
Necessary infrastructure, EVMs constitute a part of which, should therefor be in place at the 
time of holding elections. The Commission should chalk out a definite time-frame for 
upgradation and procurement of EVMs. As re gards funds, the Committee hopes that after a 
decision is taken in the meeting of all St ate Election Commissioners at Hyderabad, the 
Commission would pursue the matter with the Gov ernment so that achiev ement of targets of 
replacement/ upgradation and procurement of EVMs are not impeded in any way.  
Electors Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) 
7.36 Issue of Photo Identity Cards to voters is one of the constituents of the budget of the Legislative 
Department. Budget Estimates (Non-Plan) for the year 2004-05 under this heading was Rupees 100.00 
crores as compared to Rupees 72.72 crores during the current fina ncial year (2005-06). The reasons

Rs. 100.00 crores for this purpose during 2004-05 was in anticipation of an increased expenditure on 
this account by the State/Union Territory Governments prior to the General Elections to the 14th Lok 
Sabha. The reduction in the allocations for 2005-06 is to cover any carry forward liability which may 
be reported by the State/Union Territory Governments, due to expenditure incurred by the State during

7.37 The Committee notes that as on 1st January , 2005, total electors  in the country were 
67,65,66,131 and the number of the electors who have  been issued Identity Cards is 47,03,22,182 

which constitutes 69.60 per cent of  the total voters. Thus, there remains a shortfall of nearly 30 
per cent of those who are yet to be covered under the EPIC scheme. The Committee also notes 
that the Election Commission has started a campai gn for this purpose by selecting some States 
as a pilot project. The Committee feels that the Commission has no t achieved the desired goals 
despite the fact that considerable time has elap sed since the inception of the EPIC scheme. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recomme ndation (Para No. 7.5 of the 2nd Report of 
the Committee) that the Commissi on should devise a time-bo und programme for achieving 100 
per ent EPIC coverage.

Adm.I (L.D) dated 21st October, 2004. The response from the Ministry of Urban Development and
