7.40 The Committee notes with concern that allotm ent of land for building of the Institute of 
Legislative Drafting and Research, for which an  amount of Rs. 1.55 crore was kept in the 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the ye ar 2002-03, has not materialised so far. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Governme nt should take up this issue on priority 
and make all out efforts to ac quire land for construction of bu ilding for the Institute. The 
Government should also ensure that financial cons traints to materialise the proposal should not 
come in the way. 
Simplification of Legislative Language 
7.41 The Committee notes that the process of simplif ication of laws is the need of the day. 
Common law country like England has started simplifying its laws. The Committee observes 
that legislative language is o ften quite technical, intricate and incomprehensible for common 
man for whom laws are made. It feels that laws  should be drafted in national or regional 
languages to convey the purpose and intent of framing laws and all Central laws are translated 
into Hindi making the provisio ns known to the masses. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Government should explore the ways and means to simplify laws so as to be understood 
even by people having no sp ecialized knowledge of legal fo rmulations. In other words, 
Legislative Department should act as a catalyst  for launching a moveme nt for plain language 
drafting of laws and instruments of subsidiary legislation.

Provision for 50% recurring expenditure on Family Courts under Non-Plan side has been made during

8.4 The Department of Justice is a small Department having a staff strength of 37 persons only. 
The Budget Estimates and Revised Estimates of the Department for the year 2004-05 are Rs.65 lakh 
and Rs.80 lakh respectively. In the Budget Estimates 2005-06, a provision of Rs.80 lakh has been 
made. In  
2004-05 the Revised Estimate was Rs. 2.70 crore whereas the Budget Estimate for 2005-06 stands at 
Rs. 2.75 crore showing an increase of  Rs. 5 lakh proposed to be kept for family courts. On Plan side,

2004-05. The increase is mainly due to the priority  to computerisation of Metro/Capital City/District 
Courts and below. 
Plan  Schemes 
 Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to in frastructural facilities for the judiciary. 
8.5 The Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the development of infrastructure facilities for the 
judiciary is being implemented by this Department since 1993-94. The scheme includes construction 
of court-buildings and residential accommodation for judicial officers/judges covering High Courts 
and Subordinate Courts. The expenditure on the sc heme is shared by the Central and the State 
Governments on 50:50 basis. The Central share is however restricted to the allocations made as per 
criterion laid down by the Planning Commission. However, the States are free to spend more amount. 
Expenditure in respect of the Union Territories is fully met by the Centre. 
8.6 From 1993-94 upto 2003-04, an amount of Rs. 631.39 crore has been released to various 
States/UTs. With the matching States’ share, (Union  Territories are not required to provide matching 
share) the States/UTs were required to spend an amount of Rs. 1071.12 crore on the basis of release 
upto 2002-03. The State Governments/Union Territories are expected to submit the Utilization 
Certificates within 18 months from the date of release of an amount. Against this, the State 
Governments and Union Territories have spent an amount of Rs. 1162.34 crore upto 31.12.2004. 
8.7 So far, 69 extension buildings in various High Courts have been completed and work on 8 
extension buildings is in progress. About 107 judges’ residences of various High Courts have been 
completed and work in respect of 151 residences is going on. As regards Subordinate Judiciary, 917 
District/Subordinate Court complexes have been completed and construction work on 935 
District/Subordinate Courts is in progress. As many  as 1727 residential quarters for judicial officers 
have been completed whereas work on 1300 residential quarters is in progress. 
8.8 The Committee feels that the Centrally Spons ored Scheme relating  to infrastructural 
facilities though started in 199 3-94 has not been executed effect ively due to the absence of a 

proper planning. Similarly, extension of State G overnments’ matching share for the scheme has 
been a problem area. Consequently, the success of  implementation of the scheme has not been 
assessed properly. As informed by the Departme nt of Justice, there was no focussed or final 
targets for completion of physical infrastructu re, and States have defaulted in providing 
matching share in time. It ha s been decided on the advice of the Planning Commission to 
prepare a 10 year perspective plan for the re quired physical infrastructure State-wise. The 
Committee welcomes the move of the Government but at the same  time it cautions that the 
perspective plan should not be a mere pretext to lengthen the implementation of the scheme. 
There should be proper monitoring of the scheme in terms of achievement of targets, allocation 
of funds etc. This is more so because the Commi ttee has been given to understand that even the 
basic infrastructural facilities li ke transport and Housing are not available to the Magistrates 
and Judges at lower judiciary level and they have to encounter many difficulties. These 
infrastructural lacunae may hamper in a g reat way, their functioning. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Government should consider all these components seriously and 
include them in the ten-year perspective plan. 
Computerisation of Judiciary 
8.9 The Committee has been apprised that an improved case management technique and extensive 
computerisation have reduced Supreme Court’s arr ears from 1.05 lakh cases in 1991 to 29,315 cases 
in July, 2004. As regards pace of computerisation in High Courts and subor dinate Courts it requires 
upgradation and new-generation hardware. The computerization of subordinate courts, civil and 
criminal, has been implemented so far in two stages. About 700 city courts in four metros such as 
Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai have been comp uterized at a cost of Rs. 17.26 crore. Another 
900 courts located in State capitals, or in cities where the High Court is stationed, have been covered 
under computerization programme launched during 2003 -04 of the Department of Justice at a cost of 
Rs. 24.24 crore. 
8.10 There are in total 14,948 subordinate courts, in cluding 1734 Fast Track Courts, which function 
at the district-level and below. Excluding the aforesaid 1600 courts, which are being computerized by 
the Department of Justice, there is a balance of 13 ,348 courts which require Rs. 384.53 crore for their 
computerization. 
8.11 When these courts are computerized with appropriate local area network and wider area 
network, and the accessory systems are in place, then all the judicial courts in the country, from the 
apex to the lowest, will be computerized on one electronic grid. 
8.12 NIC has prepared a detailed project report for the computerization of the remaining 13,348 
courts. It will require a sum of Rs. 384.53 crore at  the estimated cost of around Rs. 3 lakh per court. 
The Department of Justice has circulated the EFC memo for approval of this project. 
8.13 In the 2004-05 budget of the Department of Jus tice, there is an outlay of Rs. 110 crore in R.E. 
out of which it is proposed to re-appropriate Rs . 103.05 crore for the computerization of 3475 
subordinate courts. The Planning Commission has provided ‘in principle’ approval for this project. 
8.14 The Planning Commission has further observed that the remaining 9873 courts may be 
computerized before the end of March, 2006. This will require additional resource of Rs. 281.48 crore. 
For the year 2005-06, an amount of Rs. 220.00 crore has been provided out of which an amount of Rs. 
214.00 crore has been earmarked for computerisation of district courts. Hence for 2006-07 an amount 
of Rs. 67.50 crore will be required for completion of the remaining courts. 
8.15 The Committee expresses satisfaction over the pa ce of computerisation of City Courts in 
four metropolitan cities of Delhi, Kolkata, Mu mbai and Chennai and in the courts located in 
State capitals or in cities where the High Courts  are stationed. The Committee, however, feels 

that the rate of computerisation  in subordinate courts including  Fast Track Courts functioning 
at district level and below need to be au gmented. The Committee is of the view that 
computerisation of 
judiciary will be an effective tool to bring down pendency of cases as has been experienced in the 
Supreme Court. The Committee therefore, recommends that the government should ensure that 
necessary budgetary allocations for this purpose should be made and the targets set to 
computerise the entire judicial system of the country are met. 
8.16 The Committee has been given to understand that  the issues like delayed Justice, arrears 
of cases in the courts and the increased flow of litigations can be addressed with proper 
management and introduction of  technology to the judicial sy stem. The Committee feels that 
while computerisation move is already on progress, it would be of immense help to the judges at 
these levels if they are provided with laptop fa cilities. In view of th e Committee, this facility 
would being in efficiency and provide effective basis for Judicial reforms as the Judges would be 
in 
a position to monitor, supervise and control cases from their initia l stages to their final disposal. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should consider providing laptops 
to the Judies of the Supreme Court and High Co urts at during the current year and explore the 
possibility, of extending this facilities in later phase to the lower judiciary.

8.18 The Committee notes that the Department in  its Explanatory Note on the Demands for 
Grants of the Department of Justice for 2005-06 has informed that 148 Family Courts have been 
set-up in the country as on date whereas in th e Action Taken Reply to the recommendation of 
the Committee contained in Para 97 of its Second Report, the Department has quoted a figure of 
153 Family Courts set-up so far. The Committee, therefore, directs the Department to be careful 
in future while presenting any information to it. The Committ ee observes that  the present 
position of constitution of th e Family Courts is not satisfac tory. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its earlier recommendation that Government should fix target for establishing at least 
one Family Court in each district so as to  resolve family disputes and related matters 
expeditiously.

8.20 The Committee notes that despite its recomme ndation (para 88, Second Report) that the 
Government should take necessa ry action in resolving the qu eries raised by the statutory 
auditors in a satisfactory ma nner, the Annual Report of the Academy for the year 2003-04 
reflects certain areas on which statutory audi tors have made adverse observations. This 
obviously shows that no concerted  efforts have been made by the Government in solving the 
queries of the statutory audi tors. The Committee, therefo re, reiterates its earlier 
recommendations calling upon the Government to take necessary action in the matter. 
Pendency of Cases 
8.21 As per the latest information available as on January, 2005, 30,151 cases were pending in the 
Supreme Court; 33,79,033 in different High Courts  and 2.35 crore cases were pending in the 
Subordinate Judiciary. 
8.22 The Government has taken the following steps to clear the pendency:— 
 (a) The Government has been constantly reviewing the accumulation of arrears in Courts. 
Besides increasing th e Judges’ strength from time to time, various steps have been 
taken by the Courts, viz; grouping of cases involving common questions of law, 
constitution of specialized benches and organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals, 
etc. 
 (b) The Government has also encouraged alternative modes of disposal including 
mediation, negotiation and arbitration. Special tribunals like Central Administrative 
Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family 
Courts, Labour Courts, Consumer Courts etc. have been set up to expedite disposal of 
cases. Information technology is being used in generation of cause lists, providing 
information to the 
litigants/Advocates etc. for speedy disposal of cases. 
 (c) Fast Track Courts (FTC) for the disposal  of long pending cases, particularly sessions 
cases and cases involving undertrials in jails are being set up. 
 (d) Central Government has sanctioned a grant of Rs. 502.90 crore, based on the 
recommendations of the Eleventh Finance Commission, for the creation of 1734 Fast 
Track Courts in the country. 
8.23 The Committee on Home Affairs and the Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and 
Justice in their 101st and 2
nd
 Reports, respectively, on Demands for Grants for 2003-04 and 2004-05 
of the Department of Justice had urged upon the Government to consider fresh initiatives to arrest 
pendency of cases in various courts. Government had initiated some measures to arrest and clear such 
pendency. It had also requested the State Governments/High Courts to earmark a portion of the Fast 
Track Courts to dispose of senior citizen’s cases, on priority basis. 
8.24 The Committee notes that notwithstanding its persistent reco mmendations to reduce 
pendency of cases before the Supreme Court, High  Courts and the various subordinate courts 
all over the country, there has not been any majo r breakthrough in the matter. Year after year, 
pendency of cases is increasing except the Sup reme Court where pendency has been arrested to 

some extent due to extensive co mputerisation and a host of ot her initiates. The Committee has 
been apprised that the Governme nt has been constantly reviewin g the accumulation of arrears 
in Courts and the problem is sought to be tack led by constitution of specialized benches and 
organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals;  encouraging alternative modes of disposal, 
establishing Fast Track Courts etc. The Committee finds that specialised benches, Lok Adalats 
and Fast Track courts though created as an alternative mode of disposal of arrears of cases have 
been suffering due to infrastruc tural lacuna or financial constr aints and thus are not able to 
meet the desired targets. The Committee, therefo re, calls upon the Government to address the 
problem of pendency of cases by carefully analysing the factors responsible and searching viable 
solutions in addition to the existing arrangements. 
Vacancies of Judges 
8.25 As against the sanctioned strength of 26 Judg es, the Supreme Court of India has 24 Judges in 
position, leaving two vacancies to be filled up, as on 23.3.2005. 
8.26 In the High Courts, against the sanctioned strength of 668 Judges, 527 Judges are in position, 
leaving 141 vacancies to be filled up, as on 22.3.2005. 
8.27 Pursuant to the Supreme Court Judgement of October 6, 1993, read with their Advisory 
Opinion of October 28, 1998, the process of initiation of proposal for appointment of Judges of 
Supreme Court lies with the Chief Justice of India and for appointment of Judges in a High Court, it 
lies with the Chief Justices of respective High Courts. The Government has been requesting the Chief 
Justices of the High Courts, Chief Ministers and Governors of the States, from time to time, to initiate 
proposals for filling up of the present as well as the anticipated vacancies, during the next six months. 
8.28 The Committee held detailed deliberations on the procedure for filling up of vacant posts of 
judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts, as per the pre and post 1993 dispensations. 
The Committee noted that this issue has been engaging the attention of the Committee on Home 
Affairs since long, as also of the present Committee. The Committee on Home Affairs examined the 
subject in detail in its Eight-fifth Report on Laws Delay: Arrears in Courts. That Committee was, inter 
alia, of the view that the delays in  judicial appointment was a matter of serious public concern and 
pointed out that the failure to fill up judicial vacancies promptly could not be shielded or defended in 
the name of judicial independence (para 32.2 ibid) 
8.29 The Committee observes that there has not been any perceptible improvement in the 
position of vacancies of Judges in Supreme Court and High Courts under the post 1993 
arrangement. The Committee feels that time ha s come when the issue has not only to be 
deliberated at the highest level, but also to be  debated in the public domain so that there could 
emerge an alternative system wh ich could bring about an overall improvement in the situation. 
The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Gove rnment to come forward with a concrete 
alternative, 
addressing the issue of appointment of Judges of the higher judiciary, so that the vacancies 
could be filled up on the date of their occurrence. 
8.30 The Committee felt that the increased workload  of Judges in the light of mounting arrears 
of cases also needs to be addressed seriousl y and it calls upon the Government to make a 
thorough assessment of the personnel requirement for administration of Justice and come out 
with concrete proposals to improve the situation in this regard. 
Benches of Supreme Court 
8.31 The Committee has been recommending time and again for setting up of benches of the 
Supreme Court in far-flung areas, with a view to  providing justice to th e poor, for whom it is 
impossible to visit the national capital. The Committee’s recommendations for setting up of benches 

of Supreme Court in Southern, Western and North-Ea stera parts of the countr y have been considered 
by the Supreme Court and they found no justification in setting up benches of the Supreme Court. 
8.32 The Committee, in its Second Report, dealt with the issue and felt that establishment of benches 
of Supreme Court in Southern, Western and North-Ea stern parts of the country would facilitate the 
litigants to avail justice from the apex court, wi thout traveling to Delhi from far away places. The 
Committee, accordingly, recommended that Government should decide its course of action to resolve 
the matter expeditiously. 
8.33 In its Action Taken reply to the above recommendation, Department of Justice has informed the 
Committee that the subject matter of establishing benches of the Supreme Court in other parts of the 
country was discussed in a full meeting of the Hon’ble Judges and that the full court is of the 
considered opinion that the demand for establishment of the benches of the Supreme Court can not be 
accepted. 
8.34 The Committee is unhappy with the persistent opposition for establishing benches of the 
Supreme Court in other parts of the country with out giving any reasons or justification. The 
Committee endorses its earlier view that esta blishment of benches of the Supreme Court in 
other parts of the country would be of immense help to the poor who cannot afford to travel 
from their native places to Delhi. The Committe e, therefore, impresses upon the Government to 
discuss this issue once again with the Supreme Court and explore the possibility of establishing a 
bench of the Supreme Court in Chennai at least on experimental basis and thereafter, upon its 
success, in other parts of the country in future. 
Fast Track Courts 
8.35 The Eleventh Finance Commission had sanctioned setting up of 1734 Fast Track Courts, for 
expeditious trial of long pending sessions cases and also cases involving under trials, who remain in 
jails for a period of more than two years. By the clues of the financial year 2004-05, 1549 courts had 
become functional. They have disposed 6,80,230 cases, out of 13,14,477 cases, transferred to them. 
The Fast Track Courts were started on the basis of the recommendation by the Eleventh Finance 
Commission for the period 2000-05. 
8.36 Eleventh Finance Commission had approved a total grant of Rs. 502.90 crore for 
1734 Fast Track Courts in the States. Grants fo r Fast Track Courts were one of the twelve 
upgradation grants recommended by the Eleventh Finance Commission. An amount of 
Rs. 433.75 crore has been released as grants until 28th March, 2005 and Rs. 301.48 crore 
reported as utilised. 
8.37 On query about the responsibility for releasing funds and monitoring the progress of Fast Track 
Courts, the representative of the Department of Expenditure informed the Committee in its sitting held 
on 30th March, 2005 that the primary responsibility of implementing the scheme rested with the State 
Governments and for the purpose the funds as recommended by the Eleventh Finance Commission 
were released by the Ministry of Finance. Si nce the Eleventh Finance Commission was appointed 
under 
Article 280 of the Constitution for a fixed tenure of five years i.e. upto 31st March, 2005. Thereafter, 
the new regime would start under the Twelft h Finance Commission. The Eleventh Finance 
Commission had specifically stated in its main Report that any non- plan balance as on 31st March, 
2005 would lapse. In Supplementary Report, it was stated that unspent balances might be transferred 
to the incentive fund which was given to the States. The representative of the Department of 
Expenditure further stated that States were getting a much larger chunk of money from the Centre and 
therefore, they should be in a position to take care of all the requirements including for Fast Track 
Courts. In view of the situation that would arise after 31st March, 2005, some concrete decision would 
have to be taken by the Department of Justice and the Department of Expenditure to resolve this 
issues. The Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) did not formulate any scheme on its 

own. The Department of Expenditure had not received any scheme or any budget proposal for the next 
year for the continuation of this scheme. 
8.38 On a specific query as to why the Department of Justice did not consider constitution of Fast 
Track Courts as plan or non-plan scheme and why suitable provisions could not be made, the Home 
Secretary, deposing on behalf of the Department of  Justice stated that cons titution of Fast Track 
Courts was not a plan scheme at all. It was outside the budget of the Department of Justice. The 
representative of the Department of Justice a ppeared before the Twelfth Finance Commission with 
certain suggestions and made a case for continued funding of already established Fast Track Courts 
and for setting up new Fast Track Courts through the Finance Commission grants. The problem, 
however, was that the Report of the Twelfth Financ e Commission came to the Department of Justice 
late after it was laid on the table of the Houses of Parliament. As there was no time to examine the 
Report the nature of the recommendation could not be known. Had the recommendation been received 
six months in advance, the Department of Justice would have formulated its views and schemes on it 
Fast Track Courts. 
8.39 The Committee was also informed that unspent  fund remaining in any of the upgradation 
grants, including grants for Fast Track Courts and local bodies grants are to be transferred to the Fiscal 
Reforms Facility and distributed amongst the States, which are able to reduce revenue deficit by 25% 
over five years. Finance Ministry has been approached by various States for extension of upgradation 
grants beyond 31st March, 2005. However, the Finance Ministry has apprised the States that these 
grants cannot be allowed to be used beyond 31st March, 2005. Commenting on the role of the States 
in this regard, the representative of the Department of Expenditure stated that the State Governments 
would be equally concerned about this issue since implementation of this scheme rested with the State 
Governments. The Central Government was assisting the States in that function. Hence, the State 
Governments could, for an interim period, the period in which a proper scheme is formulated, meet 
the expenditure. 
8.40 Having heard the views of representatives of the Department of Justice and the 
Department of Expenditure and having consider ed the relevant information presented to the 
Committee on the issue of Fast Track Courts, it observes that the Eleventh Finance Commission 
recommended for constitution of Fa st Track Courts as an interim measure for a limited period 
of five years to reduce pendency of cases and th e scheme has reportedly  been quite successful. 
Even the Supreme Court of India has also appreci ated the work of Fast Track Courts. It is, 
however, a sad state of affairs that the scheme no w seems to be in the lurch after the expiry of 
the term of the Eleventh Finance Commission as there is no mention of any recommendation for 
continuity of the scheme in the Report of the Twelfth Finance Commission beyond 31st March, 
2005. The Committee notes that while examining th e Demand for Grants of the Ministry of Law 
and Justice for 2004-05, the Co mmittee has been apprised that the Department of Justice had 
taken up with the Twelfth Finance Commission for continuation of the Fast Track Courts 
beyond 31st March, 2005  i.e., after expiry of the term of th e Eleventh Finance Commission. It 
appears that the Department of Justice acte d upon the assumption that Twelfth Finance 
Commission would adopt a positive approach in th is case. However, the report of the Twelfth 
Finance Commission could not be made available before finalisation of the budget process of the 
Department as a result of which the Department could not get time to pursue it further. The 
Committee feels that in these circumstances, th e Department of Justi ce should have either 
approached the Ministry of Finance with a no n-plan scheme or the Planning Commission for 
plan scheme for funding the Fast  Track Courts after 31st March,  2005, well in advance. On the 
contrary, the Department of Ju stice kept waiting for recommend ations of the Twelfth Finance 
Commission which ultimately re sulted in the present crisis.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department of Justice shou ld vigorously pursue this issue with the 

Ministry of Finance or the Planning Commission  and till the scheme is finalised, take up the 
matter with the State Governments for providing funds to be reimbursed subsequently by the 
Central Government. 
Demand No. 64 : Supreme Ccourt of India 
8.41 Demand No. 64 in the detailed Demands of Grants of the Ministry pertains to the Supreme 
Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the Supreme Court of India is ’Charged’. The total 
Budget Estimates of the Supreme Court of India fo r the year 2005-06 under the Revenue Section are 
Rs. 38.28 crore as against Rs. 38.14 crore in Revised Estimates for the year 2004-05. 
8.42 The Committee notes that the papers/documents  containing necessary  information about 
the Supreme Court and an analysis of budgetary provisions for 2005-06 we re not submitted to 
the Committee by the Department of the Justice despite the inst ructions to supply the relevant 
papers sufficiently in advance.  The Committee expresses its angu ish over this lapse and hopes 
that the Department would henceforth exercise  due care in this regard. The Committee also 
recommends that representatives of the Suprem e Court may remain present alongwith the 
representatives of the Department of Justice during the course of the deliberations of the 
Committee on Demand for Grants pertaining to the Supreme Court, for better appreciation of 
financial needs of the Apex Court. 
8.43 Some Members of the Committee raised the issue of changing the nomenclatures of the 
Madras, Calcutta and Bombay High Courts in view of the fact that after renaming of the Metropolitan 
Cities of Madras, Calcutta and Bombay as Chennai,  Kolkata and Mumbai respectively, there is a need 
to bring in corresponding changes in the names of the High Courts situated in these cities. It was 
argued that if names of these High Courts remain the same it may create confusion and mislead the 
public and appear to be anachronistic. 
8.44 The Committee therefore impresses upon th e Government to consider to initiate 
necessary action for changing the names of the Madras, Calcutta and Bo mbay High Courts in 
line with the official names of these metropolitan cities. 
Judical Reforms 
8.45 After introduction of economic reforms and globalisation and revolutionary technological 
innovations, new challenges and complexities have cropped up before Indian Judicial System 
imposing enormous burden upon the courts. As the society has become more aware, the law, the 
image of the court system and administration of justice suffer a loss of public confidence. In this 
context, it has become all the more important that the grey areas confrontin g Indian Judiciary need 
prompt attention. 
8.46 The Committee feels that it is time to consider the application of principles and techniques 
of modern management in solving some prom inent problems like law’s inordinate delays, 
arrears of cases and increased workflow in the court system. This requires scientific study of the 
problems. For this, the judiciary is required to develop skills to manage its resources, setting 
targets and evolving concepts like case management and time  management. Simultaneously 
there is need to increase output. 
8.47 The Committee has been informed that the J udges in the United Kingdom and the United 
States of America has applied so me innovative methods. These me thods have been successful in 
certain areas. For example, Annual Judicial Statistics Report, published by the Chief Justices in 
the United Kingdom and the Unit ed States every year, help to  enable the public to understand 
the performance of the judiciary. Similarly, in the United States, every Bill is accompanied by 
Judicial Impact Statement describing the likely effect of the legislation upon the workload of 
the courts. The Committee also notes that the Electronic Judicial Reso urce Management is 
gaining importance and it has been found the most effective tool for  judicial reforms. In Indian 

context, no new legislation is  required as the Information Technology Act 2000 has already 
incorporated the requisite provisions. 
8.48 The Committee is of the view th at the above measures would have significant impact on 
reforming the Indian Judicial System and th e Government should, therefore, explore the 
possibility of introducing these methods.

CHAPTER-I
OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the nodal Ministry responsible
for personnel matters, especially in respect of issues concerning recruitment, training, career development,
staff welfare, administrative reforms and post retirement dispensation. This Ministry is under the direct
charge of the Prime Minister of India, assisted by a Minister of State.
1.1. The Ministry comprises of the following three Departments:
(i) Department of Personnel and Training;
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances; and
(iii) Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare.
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING
1.2 The vision of the Department is to develop an enabling environment for the development and
management of human resources of the Government for efficient, effective, accountable, responsive
and transparent governance.
1.3 The Department’s mission is:
(i) Providing a dynamic framework of personnel policies and procedures for the effective
functioning of the Government.
(ii) Developing competence and innovation in Government.
(iii) Building capacity of human resources at all levels of Government for efficient delivery
of public services.
(iv) Inculcating and supporting a culture of transparency, accountability and zero tolerance of
corruption in public affairs.
(v) Institutionalizing a system for a constructive ongoing engagement with stakeholders.
1.4 The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) acts as the formulator of policies pertaining
to recruitment, regulation of service conditions, and deputation of personnel, besides advising all
organisations of the Central Government on issues pertaining to personnel management.
1.5 The Department is entrusted with the work relating to framing/interpretation of rules and
regulations relating to service matters; recruitment, promotion and reservation policy; induction,
training and refresher courses for all levels including senior and middle management level; service
conditions, vigilance, discipline, career and manpower planning, implementation of Right to Information
Act, 2005 etc.
1.6 The Department of Personnel and Training under the charge of Secretary (Personnel) comprises
of six wings, namely: Establishment Officer, Services and Vigilance, Establishment, Administrative
Tribunal and Administration and Training and Central Services. Each of these wings is headed by an
officer of the rank of Joint Secretary or an Additional Secretary.

2
1.7 The Department also has under its administrative control four attached offices, namely:
(i) Staff Selection Commission (SSC) : Set up by a Resolution of the Government and is
entrusted with the conduct of examinations for recruitment of lower grade staff in
Central Ministries/Departments, etc.;
(ii) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM) : A multi-disciplinary
organization specializing in capacity building, consultancy and research support, particularly
for the Central Secretariat;
(iii) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie :
India’s premier institution dedicated to training Officers of the country’s higher civil
services; and
(iv) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) : Entrusted with the investigation and prosecution
in corruption cases against public servants, private persons, firms and other cases of
serious crimes.
1.8 The other offices under the administrative control of the DoPT are:
(i) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) – a Constitutional body responsible for
conducting examination for appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under
the Union Government including recruitment to the All India Services. UPSC is created
under Article 315 of the Constitution of India. The Commission’s charter of duties is
given in Articles 320 and 321 of the Constitution. In brief, it is the duty of the
Commission to conduct examinations for appointment to services of the Union and to
advise Central Government on all matters relating to framing of recruitment rules, method
of recruitment and the principles to be followed in making promotions and transfers from
one service to another. There is a provision for consulting the Commission on matters
relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed in making promotions and
transfers from one service to another and on disciplinary matters. Article 322 of the
Constitution envisages, inter-alia, that the expenses of the UPSC including salaries,
allowances and pensions payable to members and staff of the Commission shall be
‘charged’ on the Consolidated Fund of India;
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) – a statutory body empowered to inquire or
cause an inquiry or investigation on a reference made by the Central Government. It is
also empowered to exercise superintendence over the vigilance administration of the
various Central Government Ministries, Departments and organizations;
(iii) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) –  a statutory quasi-judicial body set up to look
into the grievances exclusively of public servants so as to avoid delay in redressal of their
grievances;
(iv) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) –  a body set up by a resolution of the
Central Government with the objective of evolving a sound managerial policy for the
Central Public Sector Enterprises. It is entrusted with the responsibility of making
recommendations for appointments to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executives
and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Undertakings; and
(v) Central Information Commission (CIC) –  a statutory body set up as per provisions
in the Right to Information Act, 2005 responsible for the implementation of the Act by
exercising powers conferred to it under Section 18 of the Act.
1.9. The Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for four registered societies set
up for the welfare of Government employees and their families. These societies are:–

3
(i) The Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board –  an autonomous body set up
with the purpose of promoting cultural and sports activities among Government servants;
(ii) Grih Kalyan Kendra – an autonomous body set up with the objective of taking up
various activities for welfare of Central Government employees and their dependants;
(iii) Kendriya Bhandar – a welfare project of the Government of India set up in 1963
for the benefit of Central Government employees, their families and other customers;
and
(iv) Civil Services Officers Institute – set up with the objective to provide prompt welfare
of the officers of the Civil Services and to bring them together in order to secure
complete integration of the services and to build a corps of officers imbibed with the
spirit of co-operation in all aspects of Civil Services.
1.10 Some other activities of the Department of Personnel and Training are enumerated hereunder:–
(i) Senior Appointments under the Government of India
1.11 All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the
approval of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) under the Government of India
(Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary
of the ACC. These include board level appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and
appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the ministries/departments. In
addition, all appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed
through the Establishment Officer.
(ii) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
1.12 The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making
recommendations for appointments to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executives and functional
Directors and part-time Chairman in Central Public Undertakings.
(iii) Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM)
1.13 A well structured three-tier machinery is in place for joint consultation between the Central
Government and its employees for promoting harmonious relations and securing the greatest measure
of cooperation between the Central Government and the general body of employees in matters of
common concern.The objective is to increase the efficiency of public services along with the well-
being of the employees. The three tiers of JCM are:
(i) National Council- at the apex level, functioning under the Department of Personnel and
Training;
(ii) Department Councils- functioning at Ministries’/Departments’ level; and
(iii) Office Councils- functioning at offices/ organisations under various Ministries/ Departments.
(iv) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
1.14 In spite of the elaborate system of rules and regulations which govern personnel management,
there are employees who feel aggrieved by the Government decisions. In order to provide speedy and
inexpensive justice to them, the Government set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 1985,
which now deals with all cases relating to service matters, which were previously dealt with by Courts
up to and including the High Courts.

4
(v) Staff Welfare
1.15 Realizing that improvement in the working and living conditions of the employees and their
families leads to efficiency and high morale, the Department supports various employee welfare
measures in Delhi and other cities. The Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for
four registered societies set up for the welfare of the Government employees and their families. These
societies are the Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra, Kendriya
Bhandar and Civil Services Officers Institute (CSOI). These are located in Delhi. In addition, the
Department lays down policies for departmental canteen and supports Resident Welfare Associations.
(vi) Administrative Vigilance
1.16 The Administrative Vigilance Division of the Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal
agency responsible for formulation and implementation of policies in the field of vigilance and anti-
corruption. Its main task is to oversee the Government’s programme of maintenance of discipline and
eradication of corruption from the public service. The Division lays down policies in the field of anti-
corruption and co-ordinates the efforts of various Ministries/Departments through the Anti-corruption
Action Plan.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEV ANCES
1.17 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the
Government of India for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public grievances relating to
the States in general and those pertaining to Central Government agencies, in particular. The Department
endeavors to document and disseminate successful good governance practices by way of audio-visual
media and publications. The Department also undertakes activities in the field of international exchange
and cooperation to promote public service reforms.
1.18 The vision of the Department is to facilitate pursuit of excellence in governance for the benefit
of all citizens.
1.19 The Department’s mission is to foster excellence in governance and pursuit of administrative
reforms through:–
· Improvements in government structures and processes.
· Promoting citizen-centric governance with emphasis on grievance redressal.
· Innovations in e-Governance.
· Documentation and dissemination of best practices.
1.20 The Department is headed by the Secretary, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances and Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare, assisted by an Additional Secretary, two Joint
Secretaries, five Director/Deputy Secretary and seventeen Under Secretary level officers. There are
seven Divisions in the Department namely, Administrative Reforms, Organization and Methods,
E-Governance, Documentation and Dissemination, International Cooperation, Administration and
Coordination and Public Grievances.
DEPARTMENT OF PENSION AND PENSIONERS’  WELFARE
1.21 The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare was set up in 1985 as part of the Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions to cater to the central civil pensioners across the
country. This Department is the nodal Department of the Government of India for formulation of
general policy on pension and other retirement related benefits, besides facilitating redressal of

5
grievances relating to pension and retirement benefits. The Department has taken a number of steps
over the years for streamlining the pension administration system for greater convenience and welfare
of the pensioners.
1.22 The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare administers the following Rules:
(i) CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972.
(ii) CCS (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981.
(iii) CCS (Extra-ordinary Pension) Rules, 1939.
(iv) GPF (CS) Rules, 1960.
(v) CPF (India) Rules, 1962.
1.23 In addition, formulation as well as interpretation of Rules of New Pension System in respect
of Central government employees who entered into Central Government Services on or after 01.01.2004
has also been entrusted to Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare in terms of Government
of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961.

6

CHAPTER-III
MAJOR INITIATIVES, POLICIES AND SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
3.0 While examining the Demand for Grants for the year 2013-14, the Committee also considered
the Annual Report of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pension for the year 2012-13.
The Committee took note of the major initiatives including the legislative measures, policy initiatives
and the schemes relating to the matters under jurisdiction of the Ministry. The succeeding paragraphs
of the Report deal with some of such matters, along with the observations/ recommendations of the
Committee thereon:
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING
National Training Policy, 2012
3.1 The Committee noted from the Annual Report (2012-13) of the Ministry that the National
Training Policy, 2012 has been circulated to all Ministries/Departments, Government of India for
adoption. The policy has been formulated to strengthen the institutional mechanism for capacity
building measures for civil servants to face the emerging challenges in the changed environment in all
spheres of governance. The policy has been drafted with a view to matching individual‘s competencies
with the jobs they have to perform and bridge the competency gaps for current and future roles
through training and capacity building. Guidelines for implementation of the Policy especially on
preparing Cadre Training Plan (CTP), Annual Training Plan (ATP) etc. have been issued on 04.07.2012.
3.2 The Secretary, Department of Personnel and Training, while placing the Demands for Grants
(2013-14) of his Department before the Committee, stressed upon the relevance of the policy as
follows:
....We have not been training our lower level officials, especially, Group C and Group D at
all in most Departments. Group B officers get a little bit training at the beginning of their
career, and, after that, there is nothing. For Group A, there is a little more training. Now we
want to spread this whole thing down the line right to the lowest level, from the top, to see
that everybody should be trained three or four times a year. Our estimation is that it will cost
2.5 per cent of the salary budget.....
3.3 The Committee appreciates the new training policy framed by the Ministry. The Committee
recognizes the importance of training in the scheme of personnel administration and hopes
that the implementation of this policy would effectively bridge, through training, the likely
gaps, between the present roles performed by the Government employees and future roles to
be executed by them. The Committee also expects an improved efficiency in Governments
functioning as a result of the implementation of the new training policy.

Competency Framework for Civil Services
3.29 The Ministry, in its Annual Report, has stated thus:
As part of collaboration between the Government of India and UNDP , the “Pathways for an
Inclusive Indian Administration” (PIIA) project is being implemented by the Department of
Personnel and Training, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions with funding
from UNDP . The PIIA project focuses on developing the capacities of civil servants and on
strengthening their enabling environment in view of a more effective, efficient, transparent and
accountable Public Administration at National and State level that takes to heart the Government
of India objective of inclusion through an enhanced delivery of services to the marginalised
and vulnerable. One of the objectives of the project is to support the shift towards the
Competency–based Human Resource Management of the Indian Civil Services.

16
A draft competency dictionary has been developed during Phase I of the project through
extensive consultation with multiple stakeholders including Secretaries to the Government of
India, Chief Secretaries and Secretaries of States, PM Award Winners and other senior civil
servants. As the initiative is led by the Department of Personnel and Training, it has been
actively involved in the design of the competency dictionary from the very beginning.
Phase II of the project is now being initiated whereby Competency–based HRM will be
introduced at two pilot departments, namely, the Department of Personnel and Training and
the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. As part of pilots at two Departments, job descriptions will
be developed for all unique positions and competency requirements will be identified for these
roles.
3.30 While appreciating the efforts made by the Department to put in place a competency
framework for improving the decision making processes in the administration, the Committee
would like to emphasize upon the imperative need to impart to the Members of the Civil
Services, core human values and empathy to the problems faced by common man.

Post-retirement jobs
3.46 In the Annual Report of the Ministry, it has been stated that as per Rule 26 of the All India

sanction of the Government and that during the year 2012, permission of the Central Government has
been granted to 4 retired IAS officers for accepting commercial employment (post retirement) under

3.47 In response to a query in this regard, the Ministry has enumerated the circumstances under
which a pensioner retired from All India Services is granted permission for accepting commercial
employment within one year, from the date of retirement as follows:–
(i) Whether the organization the pensioner proposes to join has any conflict of interest or
activities prejudicial to India’ s foreign relations, national security and domestic harmony;
and whether the organization is undertaking any form of intelligence gathering;
(ii) Whether the pensioner has been privy to sensitive or strategic information in the last
three years of his service which is directly related to the areas of interest or work of the
organization which he proposes to join or the areas in which he proposes to practice/
result;
(iii) Whether there is conflict of interest between policies of the office(s) held by the pensioner
during the last three years and the interest represented or work undertaken by the

19
organizations he proposes to join. Such conflict of interest, however, should not be
interpreted narrowly to mean normal economic competition with Government or its
Undertakings;
(iv) Whether the service record of the pensioner is clear, particularly with respect to integrity
and dealings with Non-Government Organizations;
(v) The emoluments offered by the proposed employer to the pensioner and whether the
proposed emoluments and pecuniary benefits are far in excess of those currently prevalent
in the Industry. (The work “far in excess” should not be narrowly interpreted to cover
increases in such benefits that may be result of buoyancy in the industry or in the
economy as a whole); and
(vi) Any other relevant factors.

CHAPTER-IV
4.0 In the present era of increased transparency and accountability, the role played by the three
sentinels of good governance viz., CVC, CBI and CIC assume great significance, and the recruitment
agencies viz., UPSC and SSC.
CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
4.1 The Committee, while examining the Demands for Grants, had an opportunity to peruse the
Annual Report of CVC (2011). In the process, the Committee considered the following issues:
Chief Vigilance Officers
4.2 The Committee took note that as on date, six Departments of the Government of India,
(i.e. CBDT, CBEC, Department of Telecom, Department of Posts, Ministry of Railways and CPWD)
and a majority of the Public Sector Enterprises, Public Sector Banks and Insurance Companies have
full time CVOs while others have only part-time CVOs. The functions of CVOs in other organisations
are performed by part time CVOs who are officers of appropriate level from within the organizations
concerned.
4.3 The Ministry, in its reply furnished to the Committee, has stated that there were 201 posts of
full time CVOs. Out of these 201, three organizations namely (1) National Small Industries Corporation
(NSIC), (2) Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Limited (IDPL) and (3) State Bank of Indore have been
removed from the list. At present there are 198 full time CVOs.
4.4. Also, the Annual Report of the CVC states that at the close of the year 2011, 16987 complaints
were pending with the CVOs concerned for investigation, out of which 6910 complaints were pending
beyond a period of six (6) months.
4.5 The Committee is not satisfied with the current situation that only six Departments of
the Government of India have full time CVOs. The Committee is of the considered view that
CVOs play a vital role in the vigilance mechanism of an Organisation. In order to ensure
financial transparency and accountability, appointment of full time CVOs is an absolute
necessity, so that they can devote their entire time to strengthen the vigilance mechanism and
also ensure  timely disposal of complaints received.
4.6 The Committee strongly recommends that CVC should pursue the matter vigorously
with all the remaining Departments/Ministries and that DoPT should impress upon the Ministries
to take urgent steps to appoint full time CVOs.
4.7 The Committee desires that the CVC should closely monitor the disposal of cases by
CVOs and that necessary assistance/guidance may be given to CVOs to ensure zero pendency,
keeping in view the need for quick and effective action. Most importantly, the Committee
would like the network of the CVOs  in the Government Departments/Organizations to be
truly effective, meeting the purpose for which the institution has been set up. For this
purpose, there should be the requisite and desired support and protection from the CVC to
enable the CVOs to discharge their functions objectively and fearlessly.
4.8 In the Annual Report of the Ministry for 2012-13, it has been stated that the cases of
disagreement between the CVC/CBI and Sanctioning/Disciplinary Authority in the matter of Prosecution

26

prosecution shall be taken by the Competent Authorities concerned even in cases wherein they decide
to differ with CVC’s advice after obtaining views of DoPT which may be taken into account

Commission failed to seek the Commission’s advice in vigilance related matters with respect to officers
under the Commission’s normal or mandatory jurisdiction. Secondly, unwillingness on the part of
organization to accept the Commission’s advice against some officers also constitutes cases of

would prima-facie seem to be an attempt by the concerned disciplinary authorities to favour/ dis-
favour certain officers and reflect adversely on the creditability, objectivity and impartiality of vigilance
administrations. Whenever, such cases come to the notice of the Commission, its concerns are
conveyed to the organizations concerned.
4.13 The Committee is disappointed to note that, as reflected in the Annual Report of CVC,
in some of the cases, either the due consultation process with the Commission have not been
followed despite the fact that the suspected public servants were falling within the categories

4.24 The Committee noted that the amount of recovery effected in the year 2010 was R58.70
crores; that in 2011 was R88.90 crores and in 2012, it was to the tune of R151.20 crores.
4.25 The Committee appreciates the efforts made in this regard.
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
4.26 The Committee was apprised by the Director, CBI during his deposition before the Committee
that for the year 2013-14, though the demand made by CBI was to the tune of R425.36 crore, the
allocated amount was only R387.82 crore, which would mean a shortfall of 8.85%.
4.27 The Committee takes note of the shortfall in the allocation made. It would like to
impress upon the Ministry that adequate care should be taken to ensure that shortage of funds
would not be a roadblock in the modernization and effective functioning of CBI.
Conviction rate
4.28 In the Annual Report (2012) of CBI, it has been stated that during the year 2012, courts
delivered judgments in 1188 court cases. Out of these, 743 cases resulted in conviction, 345 in
acquittal, 20 in discharge and 80 cases were disposed of for other reasons. The conviction rate in
CBI cases was, therefore, 67%.
4.29 The Committee notes the conviction  rate in CBI cases.
Anti-Human Trafficking Cell
4.30 The Committee was apprised that the proposal to set up Anti-Human Trafficking Cell was
under consideration with the DoPT and that meanwhile, an existing unit has been converted into AHT
Cell w.e.f. January, 2012.
4.31 The Committee desires that the consideration of the proposal may be expedited and
that the genuine demand made by CBI may be acceded to timely.
Forensic support
4.32 As regards the setting up of forensic labs, the Director, CBI while deposing before the
Committee apprised that:

29
“..What we have done recently is that there are many forensic science laboratories run by the
private sector. They are in the private sector, but their examination report is also admissible
in the court of law. So, now, we are outsourcing our exhibits for examination...”
4.33 Taking into account the sensitive nature of the cases dealt with by CBI, the Committee
advocates the need for full-fledged forensic labs at the disposal of CBI.
Vacancies in CBI
4.34 According to the Annual Report of CBI, the total sanctioned strength of CBI as on
31
st December, 2012 was 6586 against which 5755 officers were in position with 831 posts lying
vacant. The vacancies existed in the ranks of Special/Additional Director (1), Joint Director (1),
Deputy Inspector General of Police (13), Superintendent of Police (27), Additional Superintendent of
Police (17), Deputy Superintendent of Police (137), Inspector (124), Sub-Inspector (68), Assistant
Sub-Inspector (17), and Head Constable (26). The posts of 54 Law Officers and 94 Technical
Officers at various levels were also lying vacant.
4.35 The Committee further took note of the Ministry’s reply that CBI kept making all out efforts
to fill these vacancies but the codal formalities for inducting officers on deputation took considerable
time with the result that at times there appeared to be a gap between the number of employees in
position and sanctioned strength. Besides, after final selection relieving of officers from their parent
cadre also took considerable time.
4.36 The Committee recognizes the difficulties faced by CBI in getting Officers/personnel on
deputation. However, the Committee had, on earlier occasions, in its 24
th, 38 th and 51 st Reports
recommended that if vacancies prevail due to non-availability of officers on deputation, these
may be filled up by taking recourse to direct recruitment or promotion. However, the
Committee is unhappy to note that not much has been done in this direction. The Committee
wishes to drive home the point that a premier investigating agency such as CBI should have
an independent and proficient departmental Cadre of its own, rather than being dependent on
the States and other Organisations to spare their Officers/personnel for deputation in CBI.
4.37 At this juncture, the Committee’s attention was drawn to the reply furnished by CBI that no
direct recruitment had been made in the rank of Constable in CBI since 2004 and that there was no
Direct Recruitment in the ranks of Head Constable or ASI in CBI. It was further stated that no direct
recruitment had been made in the rank of DSP during the last 10 years. The Committee was informed
by the Director, CBI that at present, direct recruitment was made only for the rank of Sub Inspector.
4.38 The Committee fails to understand as to how the vacancy position can be expected to
improve by not resorting to direct recruitment at such levels.
4.39 While expressing concern about the vacancies in CBI, one of the Members of the Committee
said that:
“...The second one is relating to vacancies. Much has been discussed. Do you have any
guidelines for those people who want to enter into the CBI? If not, there should be separate
guidelines to get into the CBI. You have to be professionally competent and highly technical
force, apart from being getting people from IPS… If you look at the outcome of the discussion
here, you need to lift up the entire status of the CBI given the socio-economic transformation
and the type of cases you are asked to handle. That sort of planning, especially by using
technology, has not been found in the Budget proposals. You are only doing regular investigation
like any other investigative agency. You are supposed to be an elite agency. There are some
recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committees. You should lift up the status of
this institution at par with international investigative agencies...”

30
4.40 The Committee also took note that as per the existing Recruitment Rules, the deputation quota
in the various Executive ranks in CBI is, viz., Constable-60%; Head Constable-20%; ASI-25%;
Inspector-50%; Dy. SP-50%; Addl. SP-10%; Supdt. of Police-60%; DIG-75%; Joint Director-80%;
SD/AD CBI : 100%; and Director, CBI : 100%.
4.41 The Committee is unable to comprehend the reason for fixing such a high percentage
as the quota for deputation in the ranks from Constable to Joint Director. The Committee is
apprehensive that the policy of not opting for direct recruitment in the ranks of Constable and
Dy. SP would, in the long run, lead to a situation wherein CBI would be totally dependent on
other Departments/States for their personnel. Therefore, the Committee recommends that this
policy should be re-looked and the Committee may be apprised of the action taken in this
regard in the Ministry’s Action Taken Reply.
4.42 The Committee does recognize the utility and the desirability to have deputation as one
of the channel to have manpower in the CBI. Deputationists  bring in a different exposure into
the organization. But, the Committee is more than convinced that the Organization should
never be dominant by the deputationists as such a state would never be congenial for the
functioning of CBI in the desired spirit. The CBI should have  strong cadres of their own at
all levels so that it can implement its procedures and practices discretely, uniformly, confidently
and with a continuity.

although he is having an obvious edge over the deputationist, in terms of skill, experience and

Statutory back-up for CBI
4.47 The Committee, in its previous Reports, had emphasized the need for a solid statutory backing

“The appeals/complaint received from Senior Citizens or from differently abled persons in the

Application of RTI Act to entities under PPP arrangement
4.64 Regarding the application of provisions of the RTI Act to various entities under the Public
Private Partnership (PPP) arrangement, the CIC has observed, in its Annual Report that due to lack
of clarity about this at various levels and especially since the RTI Act does not expressly refer to such
bodies while defining the Public Authorities; a lot of confusion persists and such entities have, by and
large, remained outside the purview of the RTI Act. Even the Ministries and Departments concerned
in the Government do not volunteer to provide information regarding these entities by claiming that
these are private bodies outside the Government control.
4.65 In this regard, the Ministry replied that Section 2(f) of the RTI Act, 2005 enables an
information seeker to access information relating to a private body from a public authority with whom
that information is available. The information that is to be provided to the public authority by private
party in PPP could be provided under RTI. In addition, if Public services are proposed to be provided
through a Public Private Partnership (PPP), all information relating to the PPPs should be disclosed
in the public domain by the Public Authority entering into the PPP contract/concession agreement.
This should include details of the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), if any set up, detailed project reports,
concession agreements, operation and maintenance manuals and other documents generated as part of
the implementation of the PPP project. Further, information about fees, tolls, or other kinds of revenue
that may be collected under authorization from the Government, information in respect of outputs and
outcomes, process of selection of the private sector party should also be disclosed. All payments made
under the PPP project should also be disclosed, along with the purpose of making such payment.
However, the documents under the ambit of the exemption from disclosure of information under
section 8(1)(d) and 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act should not be disclosed.
4.66 The Committee is of the view that the role and responsibility of the PPP entity for
implementing the RTI Act should be clarified, in order to bring in greater transparency in
implementation of such projects. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take
appropriate action in this regard.

61. The Committee recognizes the difficulties faced by CBI in getting Officers/personnel on
deputation. However, the Committee had, on earlier occasions, in its 24th, 38th and 51st Reports

other Departments/States for their personnel. Therefore, the Committee recommends that this

regard in the Ministry’s Action Taken Reply. (Para 4.41)
64. The Committee does recognize the utility and the desirability  to have deputation as
one of the channel to have manpower in the CBI. Deputationists  bring in a different exposure
into the organization. But, the Committee is more than convinced that  the organization
should never be dominant by the deputationists as such a state would never be congenial for
the functioning of the CBI in the desired spirit. The CBI should have  strong cadres of their
own at all levels so that it can implement its procedures and practices discretely, uniformly,
confidently and with a continuity. (Para 4.42)
65. The Committee takes cognizance of the above deposition of the Director, CBI. In this
regard, the Committee strongly feels that a delinquent official/personnel should be meted out
disciplinary action, irrespective of whether he is a deputationist or cadre personnel. The
argument, that punitive action is taken against cadre personnel, while a deputationist is
merely repatriated to his parent Department, in itself, is indicative that unequal working
conditions prevail in the organization for the departmental personnel vis-a-vis the deputationists.
The Committee does not see this as a healthy trend. In Committee’s view, the above
statement of Director, CBI reflects only the state of helplessness in relation to the situation
of manpower in the CBI  which is not a desirable situation.  The Committee also desires that
Cadre personnel/officers should be given a major role in policy making. (Para 4.44)
66. Further, the Committee is disappointed to note that as reflected in the Annual Report
of CBI, deputationist officers in the rank of SP were directly promoted as DIG, whereas cadre
officers in the rank of SP were promoted as SSP only which is a lower rank. Should  the
Committee derive that the departmental officer is placed at a disadvantageous position,
although he is having an obvious edge over the deputationist, in terms of skill, experience and
expertise, owing to his continuous exposure to specialized investigation which is regularly being
done in CBI? (Para 4.45)

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel,
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee, present Sixty-first
Report on Electoral Reforms-Code of Conduct for Political Parties and Anti-Defection Law. The

Election Commission of India during elections and Anti-Defection Laws as contained in the Tenth
Schedule of the Constitution.

various political parties, NGOs, individuals and other stakeholders on the subject.

made a detailed presentation on the subject on 22
nd May, 5 th June, and 14 th June, 2013. The Deputy
